A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with efficient time-stepping methods like the Krylov iteration, are remarkably versatile, the majority of research focuses on the explicit connection between Krylov methods and preservation-based discretizations. This study aims to bridge this gap by exploring implicit connections between Krylov methods and preservation-based discretizations, and demonstrating how preserving certain properties can be achieved through modification of the Krylov method itself. Specifically, we propose several variants of the GMRES method that preserve key properties, and provide theoretical proof of their preservation properties. The proposed variants' stability is further validated through numerical experiments conducted on various partial differential equations. The resulting variants of the GMRES method are readily applicable to a broad range of preservation-based discretizations, ensuring that property preservation is maintained when applying these methods to a wide range of spatially localised and global preservation-based discretizations. The proposed variants of the GMRES method are demonstrated to preserve specific properties of the solution, including monotonicity, non-negativity, and maximum norm, across a range of test cases. The resulting variants of the GMRES method are paired with two different preservation-based spatial discretization methods, including the Local Discrete Indefinite Inner Product method and the Non-Negativity Preserving Finite Element Method, to preserve the non-negativity of the solution in two different time-dependent partial differential equations. The resulting variants of the GMRES method show comparable convergence rates to the standard GMRES method, while maintaining the preservation of the desired property, as validated through numerical experiments conducted on a range of time-dependent partial differential equations. The proposed variants of the GMRES method provide flexible and adaptable tools for preserving specific properties of the solution in time-dependent partial differential equations, and demonstrate the possibility of preserving properties through modification of the Krylov method itself, rather than through the spatial or time-stepping discretization methods. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce Adversarial Metric Learning for self-supervised scene flow estimation, leveraging metric learning and adversarial training to concentrate on precise flow estimation while ignoring less accurate motion configurations. We also examine the estimation process through a series of rigorous experiments using straightforward to complex real-world datasets, showcasing the versatility of our method. All associated code and models are publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/yuezhengcv/AdMFlow. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark stars under a strong magnetic field and finite temperature conditions. By applying the MIT bag model, we derived the spin-polarized quark star's mass-equation, taking into consideration the effects of electro-magnetic interaction, pressure from gluons, and thermal pressure. We used two models for the bag pressure's pressure-pressure diagram: a constant pressure model and a linear pressure-model. Our calculations for the spin-polarized quark star's radius, electric charge, and heat capacity were expressed in terms of the critical temperature, magnetic field strength, and temperature, pressure, and magnetic field values. We then compared these expressions to general formulas, highlighting the quark field's role in defining the star's structure. Furthermore, we analyzed various temperature and magnetic field intensity conditions to determine the spin-polarized quark star's stability. Our findings showed that the star remains stable within a certain temperature and magnetic field range, with the temperature and magnetic field intensity both contributing to the star's radius expansion. However, the rate of this expansion increases as the temperature and magnetic field intensity increase. We also discovered that the heat capacity's positive value indicates the star's thermal stability across the analyzed conditions. We found that the electrical conductance and heat capacity both have a cubic relationship with the temperature and magnetic field intensity, with the heat capacity's value being approximately twice the electrical conductance's value. We then analyzed the electrical conductance and heat capacity's values at zero temperature and magnetic field, obtaining the specific values 0.17359 for electrical conductance and 0.34718 for heat capacity. This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes interior decay, which is modeled by a parabolic equation with a singular source term and boundary control. The research aims to explore the optimal temporal control that can drive the population to extinction within a finite time frame while ensuring the solution remains smooth and the population remains non-negative. The paper demonstrates the existence of a temporal control of of a specific length that achieves this result, and the optimal control duration is characterized as being directly proportional to the square of the population's initial value. Furthermore, the paper shows that this temporal control can be realized by applying a strong boundary control to the population dynamics. The research utilizes the method of backward stochastic evolution equations in combination with the singular source term model, and the results are verified through numerical simulations. The study also discusses the relationship between the population's spatial decay and the efficiency of the temporal control, and the results are applied to a real-world example involving the control of the spread of a biological invasion. The paper concludes by examining the null controllability of a related model that includes a different type of decay, and the results are compared to those obtained in previous studies. The research was previously published in the journal Mathematics of Computation and Modeling, in a special issue dedicated to the memory of Jacques-Louis Lions. The paper is organized into six sections, starting with the statement of the problem and the underlying mathematical assumptions, and the controllability result is obtained through the application of an optimal control theory known as the first order sufficient condition for optimality. The research involves three main theorems, and the paper also discusses the null controllability of a related model that includes a different type of decay, and the results are compared to those obtained in previous studies. The paper ends with two appendices, the first of which provides the well-posedness result for the controlled population dynamics, and the second of which involves the a priori estimate for the optimal control. The success of soccer teams can largely depend on high-stakes moments like penalty kicks, given the significant scoring difference with these situations. To improve performance in such critical phases, we propose a deep reinforcement learning approach to refine players' decision-making. Our method involves a dual-action framework for penalty kicks, where the primary action determines the ball's trajectory, and the secondary action affects speed and direction. By utilizing robust expectations of opponents' behavior, we ensure our strategy remains effective even when faced with opposing teams' different tactics. Empirical results show that our method outperforms existing solutions and reflects real-world patterns, including the increased success rate when kicks are taken from the center spot. Moreover, we demonstrate how our framework can be applied to other high-stakes situations, such as free kicks and corner kicks. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghpascual/soccer_reinforce.

Our approach has the potential to significantly enhance the efficiency of time-domain seismic imaging methods and underpins future development of our research, which aims to apply this method to real-world large-scale data. Our implementation is based on the SeisBox3D framework and the algorithms are detailed in the supplementary materials. Our current research challenges are notable; however, they also offer a wide range of possible future developments, as demonstrated in the appendix. This research explores an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates cognition, a cognitive reflection surface, and D2D communication. This network enables optimal management of energy harvesting and utilization. We have formulated a complex optimization problem with an infinite number of variables, a non-compact feasible set, and blockage losses, which can be difficult to solve. However, we have derived a computationally efficient algorithm to address this challenge by leveraging new cognitive capabilities, a reflected learning method, and a hybrid architecture. This algorithm facilitates efficient data transmission, energy harvesting, and cognitive capability development. Moreover, we have analyzed our proposed algorithm's convergence properties. A realistic simulation scenario has been utilized to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm. Furthermore, we have discussed a hybrid architecture's potential benefits, including enhanced cognitive capabilities, a reflected learning approach, and a efficient energy and data transmission system. This research has implications for various networks, including D2D communication, wireless networks, and energy harvesting and transmission systems. Moreover, we have explored a D2D communication network as a specific application case study. This case study involves a single transmitter and multiple receivers and is characterized by complex optimization problems, blockage losses, and an infinite number of variables. However, we have derived a computationally efficient algorithm for this case study by leveraging new cognitive capabilities, a reflected learning method, and a hybrid architecture. This algorithm facilitates efficient data transmission, energy harvesting, and cognitive capability development. The precision of target systems such as drones, rocket trajectories, and shooting scenarios can be critical to their success, and the accurate measurement of their trajectories is essential for improvement. While two-dimensional (2D) laser anemometry is a highly effective and precise measurement method, it has a significant limitation that hinders its portable application - it requires the anemometer to be within 10 meters of the measurement subject. This research introduces a innovative approach to overcome this constraint by utilizing a single-point LDV system to measure the velocity of air particles that have been affected by the target system, and it demonstrates the feasibility of measuring 2D velocities at larger distances. The development of a numerical model allows for the interpretation of LDV readings as velocity components in 3D space, and it shows that 2D velocities can be accurately determined at distances of up to 15 meters. The validation of this method is accomplished by comparing the measured and computed 2D velocities in different scenarios. The results show that this method hinges precisely on the characteristics of the air environment and yields an accurate measurement of 2D velocities even at distances of over 10 meters. The most notable advantage of this method is that it allows for the measurement of trajectories in places with limited space, and it opens the door for the application of LDV in complex scenarios that were previously off limits. The method also yields a straightforward and effective solution for reconstructing 2D velocities from LDV readings in scenarios that are farther away. The paper concludes by outlining possible future developments and corrections to the method. To prevent the spread of misleading information, it's vital to identify articles whose facts have been altered syntactically or semantically. In this work, we focus on a specific dataset containing altered newswire articles and report on the results of using contextual language models to determine semantic alteration, as well as exploring various experimentation choices and context neural networks. Our findings demonstrate that contextual language models are effective in detecting semantic alteration, with contextualized vectors providing significant information about the alteration. Furthermore, by incorporating additional features such as sentence and word context, we can significantly improve the performance of the model. Additionally, we discovered that the challenge of distinct meanings (ambiguity) poses the greatest difficulty for contextual language models, accounting for 62% of difficult instances. This is supported by our analysis of the dataset, which shows that the majority of difficult instances involving distinct meanings involve alterations caused by word swaps. This finding is particularly relevant to improving the performance of contextual language models on the dataset, with potential approaches including developing more sophisticated methods to handle context ambiguity and implementing additional techniques to differentiate words with distinct meanings. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) occurs. In this study, we use high-resolution imaging to examine the retinal neuroepithelium in developing zebrafish to determine the underlying characteristics of IKNM. We found that, in contrast to previous findings of periodic movement, fish with a normally developing retina exhibit random movement patterns on the retinal plate. We confirmed the diffusive nature of this movement by demonstrating that the distribution of nuclei follows a gradient-like pattern in both the anterior-posterior and dorsal-ventral directions, indicating that the movement is uniform in all dimensions. We also found the rate of this movement to be approximately 0.5 microns per minute. Notably, this finding is distinct from the faster, wave-like movements observed between different retinal domains. Notably, we observe that IKNM is essential for maintaining balanced nuclear distribution across the retinal plate, and abnormal movement patterns are linked to retinal development abnormalities, indicating a level of regulation over this process by the system. We conclude that IKNM serves a crucial purpose in providing a uniform foundation for the complex layering pattern observed in the neuroepithelial retina. Furthermore, we find that the movement becomes more erratic in older fish retinas, which exhibit different layering patterns, and that the precise, diffusive movement that supports uniform nuclear distribution can be reestablished when these retinas are treated with specific chemicals to promote renewed, uniform cell layering. We believe that our findings regarding the mechanical movement of cell nuclei have implications for understanding the layering of the neuroepithelial retina, and possibly other tissues, and that further investigation is necessary to determine the underlying causes of this movement. We propose the term "nuclear migratory diffusion" to describe this process, which we found to be distinct from the wave-like movements reported by previous researchers. We also found that treating fish with chemicals that promote renewed, uniform cell layering results in the precise, diffusive movement that supports uniform nuclear distribution, and believe that our findings regarding the mechanical movement of cell nuclei have implications for understanding the layering of the neuroepithelial retina, and possibly other tissues, and that further investigation is necessary to determine the underlying causes of this movement. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2020) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. This modified logic, also known as QRE, enables the sound reasoning leading to the comparison of programs' properties, including their angles, as demonstrated in (Unruh, POPL 2020). Nonetheless, QRE exceeds the capabilities of its predecessor, the quantum relational Hoare logic, which could only compare programs' properties through the inclusion of their angular parts. The integration of expectations into the preconditions and postconditions of QRE is achieved by basing this logic on unordered pairs of angles, which are defined as the zero pairs when the input angle differs from the output angle. Furthermore, we have established that the inclusion relation among programs' angles is a sound consequence of the reasoning enabled by QRE, and we have implemented a prototype of the QRE tool to demonstrate the practical feasibility of this logic. The proposed logic and tool can be applied to a range of examples, from the verification of quantum programs to the validation of noisy quantum circuits, and even to the comparison of classical programs, as shown in (Unruh, POPL 2020). The implementation of QRE is built on top of the QuProVer framework, a quantitative verification framework specifically designed for verifying quantum programs. The current version of QRE is limited to predicting program termination and does not support the validation of program properties; however, this limitation could be removed in the future by drawing from the quantitative relational Hoare logic, which enables the prediction of program properties. The integration of QRE with QuProVer has been made open-source, and is available for download on GitHub. The development of QRE has further led to the development of an Expectation-Based Verification Strategy for the QuProVer framework, which is designed to reduce the size of the search space for the verification of noisy quantum circuits and has already been successfully applied to validate a range of noisy quantum circuits, including those with noise models previously unsolvable with the QuProVer framework. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through that single event continues to spread among community members. A complex-valued neural network model based on a Hubbard chain has been developed to demonstrate accurate sign-free calculations and precise replication of known results with both exact diagonalization and dynamical mean-field theory. By leveraging complex weights, this model ensures positivity of the density matrix, thus succeeding where real-valued networks fail due to the sign issue. Furthermore, it is shown that this complex-valued approach can be converted to a real-valued network using angle-based weight transformations, which provides insights into initializing the real-valued network to avoid the sign issue. Given any non-erasing free monoid homomorphism $\phi$ and subshift $X$, its image $\phi(X)$ possesses the same topological entropy as $X$, with complexity functions in the same growth rate category. When applying $\phi$ to the full shift $A^*$, its image is isomorphic to $X$ and shares the same entropy as $X$. However, when defining entropy for subshifts over free groups, a different property arises. For any free group basis change $\psi$, the resulting subshift $\psi(X)$ has the same entropy as $X$, but not necessarily the same complexity functions in the same growth rate category. In fact, any two growth rate categories can be distinguished using free group basis changes. Additionally, a non-erasing free group homomorphism $\theta$ preserves the entropy of the shift space $X$, but not necessarily its complexity functions in the same growth rate category. In fact, there exists a homomorphism whose associated graph has a Fibonacci structure, causing its complexity to switch from exponential to linear as the word length increases. In such cases, there are variants of $\theta$ that are erasing, making the homomorphism trivial. In the context of free group basis changes, the property of having exponential complexity is invariant, while the property of having linear complexity is not. In the process, we establish a method for determining the complexity growth rate of a subshift defined by a regular language, as well as the entropy of a so-called piecewise regular automaton. Finally, we demonstrate that the property of having linear complexity is not invariant under basis changes by examining a specific example in detail. This involves calculating the complexity of a particular free group basis change, as well as verifying that this complexity grows linearly for words of sufficiently large length. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance cross-task generalization capabilities in massive language models by incorporating an unsupervised retrieval-based augmentation framework.
In this framework, we employ masked language modeling tasks to pretrain the model, then employ retrieval to select relevant examples that bridge the target task to the model's knowledge base.
We demonstrate that this model's cross-task generalization capability is improved, and this enhancement is visible across various assessment metrics in various experiments, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and translating. Our proposed approach achieves notable improvements over existing methods with minimal additional data, model parameters, or computational requirements. The code is available at GitHub.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, the Chinese government launched a specialized team to counter misinformation. However, effective strategies for reducing speculation and fake news diffusion rely on a solid understanding of how information spreads and influences public opinion. This study divides the dynamics of rumor diffusion into initial propagation and continued spread phases, and further analyzes the shifting factors that influence spread and credibility over time. Additionally, this research assesses the diverse ways rumors can impact social influence, including both direct and indirect effects. By employing a hybrid approach that combines machine learning and experimental methods to study online rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic, our findings reveal that (1) different factors vary in significance across the infection gap, (2) creditability is more susceptible to change than spread, and (3) rumors' content classifies the degree of influence, while category determines spread and creditability separately. Moreover, this study validates the unique characteristics of the COVID-19 pandemic environment, which affect rumors' spread and creditability, and further analyzes the persistent effects of increased regulation and improved online literacy on reduced speculation and fake news diffusion. This research provides actionable recommendations for implementing targeted measures to control misinformation and provides a usable dataset for further scholarly analysis. This study's findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics of rumor diffusion, spreading strategies, and the influence of creditability, and can be applied to various misinformation scenarios beyond the COVID-19 pandemic context. This research utilizes a large-scale dataset of online rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic, which includes attributes and time stamps that allow for dynamic analysis, combined with a influential theory of innovation diffusion, to investigate the dynamics of rumor diffusion and provide actionable policy recommendations for reducing speculation and fake news diffusion. This study's findings are relevant to a broad range of domains including computer science, public health, economics, political science, and sociology. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting and analyzing a large sample of these nebulae across a wide field of view. The Fornax3D galaxy survey, which covers a $1.5^{\circ} \times 1.5^{\circ}$ region in the Fornax cluster, provides a suitable dataset for this type of research. The observation includes a comprehensive planetary nebulae catalog consisting of 845 confirmed planetary nebulae within the cluster galaxies. Using a customized automated detection method, researchers identified and examined the planetary nebulae within the data, confirming the accuracy of their results and validating the method as a reliable tool for planetary nebulae detection based on narrow-band nebular emission. The completed catalog includes the coordinates, total flux, and area of each planetary nebula, as well as an estimated brightness for each one. By analyzing the planetary nebulae within the Nuclei of Advanced Spiral Galaxies (NGC 1394 and NGC 1316), researchers avoided counting the same nebulae multiple times and accounted for the completeness of the sample. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this, we employ a simple yet effective strategy called the efficient loss selection method, leveraging a single, composite loss function consisting of a core loss function enhanced by a carefully chosen penalty term. When applied to real-world datasets, this approach delivers performance gains over conventional methods. Our work is accessible to the broader deep learning community due to its theoretical and practical aspects. Our research suggests that, in contrast to treating the loss function as a fixed constant, it's advantageous to treat it as a parameter that can be optimized, making further innovations in this area a promising direction for future work. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ghrasoul/EfficientLossSelection.

A temperature-dependent Young's modulus was introduced to simulate deformation caused by initial crystalline regions, and the effects of surface tension were addressed to prevent numerical issues. A comprehensive equation is then proposed to describe material deformation and temperature distribution, and this approach is applicable to other materials experiencing anisotropic deformation due to temperature, strain, or combination of both. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. The importance of incorporating spin-polarization of the superconducting order parameter is further illustrated by examining the influence of finite momentum pairing within a simple tight-binding model, with results showing that this type of pairing automatically leads to a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field. The relevance of these findings to other $\.k$-space complicated superconducting materials is also discussed. The approach used in this analysis, relying on the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near the critical temperature, proves to be effective in investigating the response of the superconducting state to external pressure, tension, or strain, by accounting for the anisotropic response of the superconducting state through the order parameter's gradient. The role of disorder, in the form of point defects or line defects, on the superconducting state is further examined, with results showing that spin-triplet nematic superconductivity is resistant to the influence of point defects but can be broken down by line defects, representing edge dislocations in the crystal lattice, to the superconducting state depending on the orientation of the applied stress or strain. This paper expands upon their analysis and presents a new delay power reduction expression that can be applied to a broader range of CPM signals, taking into account their cumulative distribution functions. We investigate the quantum capacity and vacuum compressibility of quantum spacetime when it is exposed to thermal environments. Using the formalism of massless minimally coupled scalar fields in (1+1) dimensional spacetime, we determine the effect of thermal sources on the quantum capacity and vacuum compressibility for two types of spacetime backgrounds: flat spacetime and spacetime with a cosine-shaped barrier. Specifically, we examine the change in these quantities for free fields in thermal states, as well as in coherent states, both in flat spacetime and in spacetime with a cosine-shaped barrier. Our study shows that coherent states generally offer greater quantum capacity and vacuum compressibility than thermal states, with the difference being more pronounced in regions close to the barrier where the gravitational well is deeper. Furthermore, we find that in flat spacetime, the change in these quantities is directly proportional to the square of the average number of field quanta. In contrast, for spacetime with a cosine-shaped barrier, the relationship is more complex due to the variation in field behavior across the barrier. We also determine the thermal temperature required to achieve a certain level of vacuum compressibility or quantum capacity, finding that it is the same for both coherent and thermal states. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between thermal environments and the quantum properties of spacetime, as well as the effectiveness of coherent states in maintaining vacuum properties in dynamically changing spacetimes. Moreover, we demonstrate that in certain situations, coherent states can offer benefits over thermal states in regulating the quantum behavior of spacetime, with implications for the use of coherent states in quantum gravity. Finally, our study highlights the importance of taking into account the interaction between the quantum field and the boundary of the spacetime region, rather than treating it as if it were isolated, as this interaction can significantly affect the behavior of the field and the background geometry. Our work also paves the way for a broader investigation of the effects of boundary conditions on the quantum field and the spacetime geometry in (2+1) dimensional spacetime. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday common-sense reasons both for and against performing various actions, described in straightforward "if-then" statements. This dataset distinguishes itself from existing sources of common sense by focusing on the reasons behind actions, rather than describing actions themselves. With over 570,000 generated "if-then" statements covering twenty diverse actions, ATOMIC provides a unique resource for advancing automatic reasoning capabilities. Our objective with this dataset is to enhance and validate automatic systems capable of making and rejecting assumptions about the world around them. We have implemented twenty examples of action-justification pairs in a model called MPA-GPT, that outperforms a simple baseline in twenty individual evaluation metrics. We have also created six diverse tasks that showcase a system's capacity to make informed decisions about what assumptions to take for granted when engaging in everyday tasks of text classification, natural language generation, and multiple choice questions. The comprehensive nature of this dataset, coupled with its distinct focus on the principles of automatic reasoning, offers a unique opportunity to advance machine intelligence in this critical area. We have made this dataset available to the public and it can be accessed at https://atOMIC.org. The code for MPA-GPT can be found at https://github.com/facebookresearch/MPA-GPT. One of the most significant advantages of quantum computing lies in its capacity to accelerate linear algebraic problems through iterative linear solvers, particularly the use of the Quantum Linear Algebra (Quantum Algebraic Manipulation) library, by executing operations in the exponent of the number of calculations. However, due to the limited number of quantum bits (qubits) available in next-generation quantum devices, certain operations cannot be performed within the device itself and may require connection to a classical system. The HHL (Harrow, Hasseler, Lloyd) algorithm stands out as a renowned example of a quantum linear solver that can't be implemented on these devices due to the challenge of constructing the necessary unitary operator, which demands an enormous amount of memory. In this research, we introduce a novel approach called NISQ-HHL, a variant of the HHL algorithm tailored for usage on devices with limited qubits. NISQ-HHL is characterized by converting the algorithm into a form that utilizes a unitary operator of more manageable size, incorporating a set of quantum amplitude amplification modules instead. We have tested this new algorithm on two applications: quantum singular value decomposition (QSVD) and quantum linear regression. The results show that NISQ-HHL outperforms the standard HHL algorithm in terms of execution time on realistic quantum hardware settings. Furthermore, we explore the integration of NISQ-HHL within the Porterfolio framework, a recently developed approach for optimizing quantum algorithms. The findings from our testing indicate that Porterfolio, when combined with NISQ-HHL, achieves superior performance compared to the standard HHL algorithm. We have made NISQ-HHL available as an open-source code on GitHub. In addition, we have outlined possible future improvements for this algorithm in the paper. The current version of NISQ-HHL is suited for applications involving relatively small-size matrices. The paper concludes by presenting a realistic scenario that demonstrates the capabilities of NISQ-HHL. The new algorithm introduced in this research has the potential to excel in a broad range of linear solver tasks, as it tackles a problem that affects a significant portion of the approximately 10,000 available quantum algorithms. The NISQ-HHL algorithm can be used to enhance the HHL algorithm, making it possible to execute the HHL algorithm on devices with a limited number of qubits, specifically those with less than 10 qubits. The paper is accompanied by a supplementary document that includes additional information about NISQ-HHL, along with the technical details regarding the Porterfolio framework

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional focus network that aligns sampling rates by utilizing strided convolutional layers in both encoders and a sample rate adaptation module, thereby enabling flexible sampling rate learning. Furthermore, a reverse attention mechanism is employed to ensure that the encoders learn representative features from each other, resulting in a bidirectional focus network that produces encoders with interchangeable outputs. This network is then used to train a speech encoder that pairs a transformer-based ASR model, which in turn trains a language encoder to produce a hidden state for the decoder. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 20% reduction in training time when the model is trained with a large amount of unpaired text data, and an 5% improvement in WER when trained on a limited dataset. Code is available at: https://github.com/ghru/bidirectional-focus-network.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The paper also discusses related lower and upper bounds for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations, providing both general and specific bounds for particular values of $k_n$. The findings related to the total variation distance have been previously obtained by Diaconis and Hicks, but the paper presents new and larger Kolmogorov distance bounds. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The observed effects also prompt an examination of the dimensions and surface morphology of the nanowires, revealing non-uniformities that may influence the electrical properties. The study indicates that both the Coulomb blockade and quantum interference effects share equal significance in describing the nanowires' conduction, suggesting that coherent quantum phase slips and Coulomb blockade coexist in the nanowires. The research involves an analytical model that incorporates both mechanisms and provides a method for determining the distribution of the nanowires' length based on their electrical characteristics, offering practical value for manufacturing and electrical property optimization. The study has implications for using nanowires for quantized circuit applications and highlights the complexity of experimental implementations. The findings are validated through comparison with existing data on nanowire arrays and alloy-based nanowires, citing the importance of considering the inherent variability of individual nanowires in place of focusing solely on average array properties. The research provides a framework for investigating the variability of other Josephson junction systems, offering a potential tool for visualizing the distribution of junction parameters in mesoscale devices. The possible connections to related phenomena, such as noise spikes and dc characteristics in mesoscale superconducting networks, are also discussed. The development of a precise quantitative model is envisioned as a future step, along with the exploration of noise-based measurement methods that may provide additional insights into the nanowires' behavior. The potential applications of the discovered noise-based parameter extraction technique are also considered, offering a potential tool for validating simulation models and validating the performance of manufactured devices. The findings may contribute value to related fields of research, including solid-state quantum computing and nano-electromechanical systems. The discovery of the complex behavior of the nanowires also raises further questions about the effectiveness of the used simulation models and the validity of the used manufacturing

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence. Although the model assumes a non-relativistic description of quarks, it provides a good fit to calculated masses to the level of 10%, and predicts additional narrow resonance states of the Ω-baryon. A comparison with the approach of the "constarized" Bethe-Salpeter method is also presented, showcasing both methods' results on magnetic moments, form factors, and decay widths. A discussion on possible production mechanisms for the Ω-baryon at various colliders is followed by a study on the hadronic decay modes using an isospin-coupling method, which provides relative decay width calculations for the ground and excited states. A comparison with the results of lattice QCD and other approaches on decay widths and hadronic masses is also included. A section on the quantum logic of quark flavors that compose the Ω-baryon particle follows, along with a discussion on the Ω-baryon's exotic nature and the underlying physics that allows it to exist. A study on the magnetic moment of the Ω-baryon particle at its ground and excited states is also presented, which may be measured using magnetic measurement tools at future experiments. A conclusion summarizes the main results of this paper, which have been applied to colliders, such as the LHC, and propose a method for detecting the Ω-baryon particle using electric monopole moments, followed by a appendices section that includes additional mathematical information.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In evaluating the utility of a 'well mixed' model, our findings suggest that it may not necessarily hold true for predicting the rate of disease transmission in bus environments, and that more refined models are necessary to accurately capture the dynamics at play. This study was motivated by the recent transmission of COVID-19 on urban buses, and the findings presented here are expected to contribute value to ongoing public health efforts by providing a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying disease transmission in similar confined environments. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, while also providing a quality score for each image. We evaluated this model on three separate datasets, utilizing previously unseen datasets for validation and testing, and found it outperformed existing baselines in various metrics. Nonetheless, room for improvement remains, as enhancing image quality further may be possible with a larger training set. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Yue Cao/phys-pet.

This study delves into the practice of training neural networks to identify these connections and investigates how the principles of the centering theory influence their performance. Our analysis takes place within massive datasets containing numerous references to entities, derived from conversational dialogue using Wikipedia articles as well as detailed literature reviews on neural networks that identify relationships between entities. The potential applications of this finding extend beyond conversational systems, perhaps even into the realm of storytelling, where the connection between characters and their surroundings can provide a richer, more immersive experience for readers. The metric dimension of a graph is a concept originally developed to describe the spatiotemporal localization of an object within a metric space. This idea has been extended to graphs, where a set of vertices represents observers who can determine the location of the object based on the connections between them. The minimum number of observers needed to uniquely identify any point in the graph is known as its metric dimension. Here, we explore new guidelines for configuring these observers to minimize the metric dimension of an unknown graph. Specifically, we investigate the scenario where the accuracy of each observer's readings has a limited time frame, unknown to the object's tracker. By leveraging this time frame, we can determine the metric dimension of an unknown graph by employing a variant of the trimmer algorithm, which gradually refines the estimate of the metric dimension or detects its impossibility in a finite number of steps. Alternatively, we show that any mapping of the graph's vertices to numbers representing the accuracy of each observer's readings will enable us to determine the metric dimension of the graph. Furthermore, we establish that the metric dimension of a graph can be determined from a representative sample of its vertices. Additionally, we provide a mathematical formula for calculating the metric dimension of a graph and demonstrate its applicability with examples. Moreover, we discuss various properties of the metric dimension of graphs, including its relationship with graph connectivity, cliques, and the size of the largest connected component. Lastly, we outline some open problems related to the metric dimension of graphs. This study was originally published in the journal Discrete Mathematics.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines multiple learning approaches to create a robust assessment of potential solutions, taking into consideration factors such as fairness and the effectiveness of the guidance. We uncover several intriguing insights regarding how the theory-of-mind of the Dungeon Master influences the outcomes of the game. Ultimately, the G4C framework and the findings presented can be applied to a broader range of tasks involving intent-based conversations and games, as well as other contextual evaluations. We make all data associated with this challenge freely available.

A novel approach using persistent topological mapping identifies the possible folding paths for a group of knotted proteins based on their three-dimensional structures. This method enables the distinction between different bending pathways, specifically identifying those that involve ring interconnection, which is crucial for defining protein knots. A study utilizing this approach maps the bending pathways of knotted protein structures and compares their overall features. It also finds that the ring interconnection pathways of protein knots contain curved segments that cannot be disentangled easily. Furthermore, by analyzing various protein knots, the study discovers that the straightening of knotted proteins often involves the modification of existing rings rather than the creation of new interconnections. Additionally, it discovers a relationship between protein knots and their folding states, revealing that the most complex knots tend to arise from folded states that are already compact and difficult to unfold. The study T also offers a theoretical framework that enables the possible folding paths of knotted proteins to be categorized based on their topological features. The research provides a novel perspective on the relationship between protein knots and their folding processes. To address this challenge, we developed a two-stage protocol in which a initial brief instruction primes the model with a condition, and the model then generates a phrase to complete a blank, as in "It's likely that ____." We found this protocol to be highly effective in improving the quality of generated hypotheticals, a improvement we measured using assessment metrics focused on content integration. The precise origin of gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting large amounts of radiation in the gamma-ray range remains unclear.  Hadronic cosmic ray collisions with disk material are an intriguing explanation, but may be limited by magnetic fields restricting the formation of disks.  We investigate the relationship between disk formation, magnetic fields, and gamma-ray activity in low-luminosity galaxies.  We analyze the relationship between the number of gamma-ray sources and factors such as star formation and luminosity, and find that a threshold of 10^44 erg/s s necessary for gamma-ray activity to appear.  We test our findings against alternative models of gamma-ray activity and star formation, and find that a combination of exponential star formation and gamma-ray activity controlled by magnetic fields provides the best fit.  We also explore the possible presence of hadronic gamma-rays in M31 and M33 using existing gamma-ray data and far-infrared observations, and estimate the total gamma-ray energy production of these galaxies in the gamma-ray range.  Finally, we discuss the possible link between gamma-ray activity and black hole growth in the context of a unified scheme of radio galaxies.  We conclude by examining the implications of our findings for the possible absence of gamma-ray activity in low-luminosity galaxies with strong magnetic fields, and the limited reach of current gamma-ray telescopes in detecting the radiation of the most obscured accretion discs. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of sound recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of noise-resilient algorithms to enumerate cardiac auscultation sounds.  From recorded sounds, features were extracted using short-term and long-term signal analysis techniques.  Experiments used two categories of noise: Gaussian and real-world background noise, and tested various noise levels to simulate different recording environments.  The study divided recorded sounds into training and testing sets and used multiple machine learning classifiers to evaluate models on the test data.  Results showed that Gaussian processes are more effective than random processes for machine learning model training on cardiac auscultation sounds.  Also, the findings indicated that model performance is sensitive to noise levels and distance between sounds.  Furthermore, the study found that Gaussian processes are more precise than statistical models in sound classification, and that cardiac auscultation sound classification using Gaussian processes is challenging due to the limited duration of sounds.  To overcome this challenge, the study proposed a segment-based approach to classify sounds.  To address the issue of recording device variability, the study proposed a second-order statistical feature extraction method to compare sounds recorded on different devices.  The proposed method extracted features from a cardiac auscultation sound database recorded with a stethoscope, an electronic device, and a mobile phone.  The method divided the recorded sounds into training and testing sets and evaluated several machine learning classifiers on the test data.  The results showed that the proposed method is capable of detecting myocardial infarction sounds recorded with an electronic device and a mobile phone as stethoscope recordings. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Typically, machine-based classification systems are trained and tested on large datasets, yet in healthcare, often only a limited dataset is available for model training. Moreover, due to data security concerns, it's common for users to keep their health data private, making data sharing challenging. Furthermore, models trained on user data without consideration for future interactions tend to have poor performance. In response to these issues, we present FedHealth, a innovative framework that leverages transfer learning within a federated learning framework for healthcare. FedHealth successfully addresses concerns around data privacy and security by enabling users to maintain their health data privately. Moreover, without access to individual data, FedHealth enables trainers to update a global model using aggregate dataset information, thereby reducing data sharing obstacles. In addition, FedHealth enhances classification accuracy for new users through successful transfer learning without compromising efficiency. In comparison tests with other baseline methods, FedHealth demonstrates superior performance in sports activity classification. In particular, FedHealth achieves approximately 8% better accuracy with 10% reduced training time in sports history classification. The proposed framework and the associated code are available at https://github.com/ChangKun/FedHealth. The development of FedHealth highlights an significant approach to dealing with data scarcity and lack of user engagement, both of which are critical concerns in healthcare. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001. It deals with a sequence of operations that generates a sequence of permutations based on the insertion or deletion of elements, and the objective is to determine the original sequence of operations. For a set of permutations generated through insertion or deletion of elements from a initial permutation, the corresponding sequence of operations is implicit. However, when the operations that generated the permutations can be either an insertion or a deletion, the original sequence is difficult to enumerate. In this paper, we outline the different cases of sequences of operations that result in the same permutation and provide a systematic approach to reconstructing the initial sequence of operations from its final permutation, along with the number of operation instances. We also examine statistical properties of the initial sequence of operations, presenting the distribution of the number of operation instances, the distribution of the first operation instance, and the most likely sequence of operations on average. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the sequence of operations and the Hamming distance between the initial and final sequences, and the related problem of determining the sequence of operations that transforms the Hamming distance between two permutations in a way that minimizes the number of element changes. We address these questions using a mathematical model that incorporates the underlying principles, and we present numerical results for sequences consisting of up to seven elements. The data allows any user to generate additional sequences. The research findings presented in this paper were concluded in 2020. The author would like to give special thanks to V. Ushakov for providing the figure, and to the National Science Foundation for funding the research through grant CCF-0917211. The sequence reconstruction issue for permutations with the Hamming distance as the cost of changing an element is distinct from the traditional sequence reconstruction problem. It has been previously unstudied and presents an interesting and novel research approach. It involves analyzing the distribution of the number of element changes, the distribution of the number of insertion or deletion events, the most likely sequence of operations on average, and the sequence of operations that transforms the Hamming distance between two permutations in a way that minimizes the number of element changes. The paper introduces an innovative method of investigating this issue using a mathematical model based on the underlying principles

We have theoretically analyzed multiple aspects of laser-induced three-body recombination from spinless dimer states, which can be realized using atom-molecule trapping systems with a 1D configuration. This process is precise and efficiently converts spinful atoms into molecules with the same parity as the initial dimer state. Our calculations demonstrate how varying the wavelength of the breaking laser, as well as the interaction between dimer states and background atoms, affects the efficiency of this process. Additionally, we have examined two scenarios: one where the initial state is a symmetric spinless dimer state, and another where the initial state is an asymmetric spinful dimer state. In both cases, our research shows that it is possible to achieve over 50% efficiency in recombining the dimer into a single molecule. Our study also illustrates how this process can be optimized by adjusting the strength of the interaction between the dimer states and the surrounding atoms, although this is more challenging for asymmetric dimer states. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that in both scenarios, combining the process with cooling techniques leads to even higher efficiency rates. Our research indicates that the lowest possible level of spinful atom-molecule conversion can be achieved within a critical parameter window, which can be minimized by adjusting the ratio of the breaking laser's intensity to its wavelength squared. Our study facilitates the implementation of this process using actual laboratory setups, and we have included a useful equation that relates the efficiency of the process to the wavelength of the breaking laser and the range of interactions between the dimer states and the surrounding atoms, based on a 3D Poisson distribution. Our findings also suggest that in both scenarios, it is possible to achieve an average molecule-molecule interaction energy that is several times greater than the temperature of the trapping system. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. We also illustrate how this approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, enabling the prediction of flow velocities in areas with changing riverbed profiles. In total, our results show that this method can predict flow velocities to a 75% accurate level with a computational cost that is 96% lower than traditional methods, leaving room for further improvement particularly in areas with significant riverbed changes. Despite these limitations, this research paves the way for a range of potential extensions and improvements, as well as various applications such as flood risk management, surf routing, and shallow water wave propagation. Moreover, the proposed framework provides a practical illustration of how to incorporate spatial data into machine learning models, which can be applied to other similar problems involving data with a spatial structure. Lastly, this research is accompanied by an open-source code and reference dataset, in addition to a series of animated plots visualizing the predicted flow velocities and riverbed profiles. This code can serve as a platform for further developments and adaptations of this model, as well as a reference for implementing similar models in other environments. This work is relevant to the MMLA framework, with connections to the PDE, data, and machine learning components, which facilitated this research as well as providing a suitable framework for interpreting its results. This research is also part of a broader project involving the development of a nonlinear Schrödinger equation solver, as well as applications to river flow velocity models with long-range dependence, and to the analysis of complex networks with dynamic nodes. HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. Since the optimal exposure spectrum depends on both the camera hardware and its surrounding environment, we researched how to determine the ideal range and how to process images for HDR production. In this research, we focus on exploiting smartphones to obtain HDR images and established a method to automatically identify the best range of exposure levels, taking into consideration the specific hardware of a particular smartphone. We also developed a fusion technique for HDR production, capturing images at the optimal exposure range to minimize light loss while reducing noise to some extent. The experimental results showed that our method delivers higher-quality HDR images compared to standard techniques and other competing apps available on the market. The proposed technique was tested on three popular smartphone models and produced notable HDR images in various challenging lighting conditions. The method has been made available online for public access. The underlying code can be found at https://github.com/ghasemzade/FuseHDR. This study conducts a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art algebraic solvers for finite element models of cardiac mechanics. We examined and compared the performance of four multilevel preconditioners: PARDISO as a solo competitor, and three other methods that combine PARDISO with two other solvers (BCG and GMRES) and two different strategies for handling non-local stiffness (alien shrink and Delaunay reordering). Our tests utilized real-sized models of human hearts and simulated material models currently at the forefront of research. Our findings were determined through computations performed on high-performance computing clusters and localized computing resources. We evaluated and compared the performance of these solvers on various scales, examining their performance on small models in detail and employing a more general comparison for larger models. Our results demonstrated that the combination of PARDISO with BCG and Delaunay reordering delivered the best performance among the methods examined, outperforming the latest solvers like ALBERT and ALBREACH for complex models of the heart. Our study is accompanied by an open-source code that allows users to replicate our results, examine the performance of these solvers on other models of the heart, and experiment with different solvers and strategies on finite element models of cardiac mechanics. Our findings have significant implications for researchers and clinicians who use computational models of cardiac mechanics, given the growing importance of simulation speed in their work. Given the flexible design of our code, our results also contribute to an ongoing research challenge known as the Solid Mechanics Suite. Our study delivers a scalable solution for the time-dependent simulation of cardiac mechanics, and our code provides a platform for further innovation in this area of research. Lastly, our results highlight the limited impact of different material models on computation performance, given the growing complexity of models and limited time spent on simulation by researchers and clinicians. High-speed flow measurements are commonly disrupted by turbulence, resulting in poorly resolved images of velocity fields. Our study utilizes a generative adversarial network to enhance the spatial resolution of velocity field maps captured in chaotic flows at different Reynolds numbers, between 2000 and 20,000. A single low-resolution image was used to create a detailed, $37\times 37$ velocity field grid, with 13 test images at various Reynolds numbers being used to train the network. The generated velocity fields in different regions were compared to actual experiments, with the standard deviation of the difference being less than 0.5 $m/s$ for most cases. The resolution enhancement model also allows for the construction of rarefied velocity fields, with the condition that the overall density remains consistent. A direct measurement approach is proposed to determine the refractive index of a complex flow, with the result from GAN matching approximately 1.03 in all cases. Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a long-duration gamma-ray signal lasting around 14 hours during the significant X2.0 solar flare on November 7, 2004. The detected radiation matched the energy spectrum of cosmic rays, specifically neutrons, and underwent expected decay over time, presenting a novel approach to measuring high-altitude solar radiation at an extreme height through ground-based observation. Furthermore, this discovery is relevant to enhancing the sensitivity of future ground-based cosmic ray monitors at higher elevations, such as the planned CREAM-2 device on Icelab at 5620 m above sea level in Chile. The observed gamma-rays also shed light on the effectiveness of solid-state recorders in securing important solar data, given their successful capture of the entire duration of the gamma-ray signal. The underlying physics has been thoroughly analyzed through numerical modeling, combining solar particle projections and neutron decay, to better understand the findings and potentially apply them to similar future observations. The associated data are publicly accessible via the University of Tübingen's website. The discovered radiation signal's prolonged duration also sparked interest in investigating recent large solar flares for similar gamma-ray signals lasting over several hours, which could provide insights into the stability of high-altitude solar radiation and facilitate comparisons with solar cycle data. The observed gamma-rays primarily fell within the 0.2-10 GeV range, which closely matched the energy spectrum of neutrons undergoing radioactive decay, specifically proton-rich isotopes like 12C, 16O, and 20Ne, which emit gamma-rays through electron capture over different time scales. The most intense radiation was detected around 10-13 hours after the solar flare, which coincided with the peak of the associated X-ray flare. The effective altitude of the radiation was determined to be around 5000 meters, which was confirmed by comparing ground-level measurements from various elevations, allowing for the calculation of the associated energy of the neutron flux. The energy of the neutron flux was approximately 6 GeV, which was determined by matching the observed gamma-ray spectrum with numerical simulations of neutron decay, also taking into account the isotopes' masses and energies. The radiation's duration and altitude stability sparked interest in investigating the system dynamics that could underpin the stability of high-altitude solar radiation, which could be relevant to extending the time frame of future ground-based cosmic ray monitors. The associated data are available via doi: 10.4070/EPhG.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex behavioral pattern in rapidly rotating low-mass stars, particularly those in the mass range of planetary bodies, where angular momentum shifts cause the near-surface layers to spin faster rather than slower. This paradox has observed manifestations in the spectral analysis of stars with planetary companions, where specific absorption lines demonstrate unusual patterns of variation. We present a comprehensive analysis of newly gathered observations from the HERMES spectrograph, combined with prior data, to reassess the phenomena observed in K2, Kepler, and CoRoLa stars. By incorporating recent advancements in precision measurements of stellar rotation, we employed the LSD technique to detect patterns of variation in the spectral lines and confirmed the unusual shifts in the stars K2-25 and EPASCOP-1, previously reported by other researchers. Additionally, we discovered similar phenomena in the stars K2-93, Kepler-45, and CoRoLa-2, and identified a possible periodicity in the stellar rotation of K2-25. Furthermore, we explored possible explanations for the observed shifts, considering the influence of magnetic cycles, oscillations, binarity, and angular momentum redistribution, and found that the data favor the latter two scenarios. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanisms remaining unclear, and the findings encourage future observational and theoretical efforts to investigate this phenomenon, perhaps through simulations of massive planetary impacts that cause the star to spin faster, and the study of other stars that may exhibit similar phenomena. Sensitive measurements of the stellar rotation period, as well as the analysis of seismic data, may provide a fuller comprehension of this behavior. The code used in this analysis has been made available at https://github.com/astrofrog/ldtool. The observations and data reduction are documented at https://research.reed.edu/~astrofrog/research/2022_JPhASp.pdf. The research was supported by the ARC, NASA, NSF, and the REU program. The authors would like to acknowledge the contributions of the HERMES team, the K2, Kepler, CoRoLa, and TESS missions, as well as the participants of the STARS SEISMIC workshop. The researchers are further grateful for the access provided to computational resources, in particular the Australian National University's ARRAI supercomputer, and the NASA's Pleiades supercomputer, and the funding for the REU program, along with the ARC and NASA grants. Quantum connections between silicon atoms are crucial for utilizing quantum entanglement in silicon-based devices. Researchers have successfully demonstrated the coupling of atomic states over distances of up to 5 nanometers. However, above this scale, quantum communication becomes interrupted by valley interference, a phenomenon inherent to silicon's crystal structure that causes deflection of entangled connections along particular paths. Until now, it was unknown how valley interference affects pairing of atomic states in planar arrangements or in three-dimensional configurations. A recent study by a team led by Dr. Rankin utilized highly precise methods to examine the behavior of paired atomic states in both planar and three-dimensional configurations, and has discovered ways that valley interference can be utilized to switch spin in silicon atoms, and has revealed the complex, varied patterns that valley interference creates in both planar and three-dimensional configurations. Recent advances in large language models have achieved high performance on various natural language processing tasks. However, incorporating structured knowledge into these models has presented a significant challenge due to the lack of suitable data and appropriate model architectures. We argue that knowledge structures, as seen in knowledge graphs, can be utilized for better understanding and representation of the world. To address the difficulty of integrating these structures, we employed a simple approach that involves creating multiple classification models to incorporate knowledge structures into language models. Our approach was applied to knowledge graphs and yielded notable improvements in model performance on link prediction and knowledge inference tasks. Additionally, we discovered that by utilizing knowledge structures as input for our model, we could accurately determine word meanings and categorize words into different classes. Our research utilized a minimal amount of data and straightforward techniques to achieve these results, and we believe it can be built upon to explore more complex methods of integrating knowledge structures into language models. Our code has been made publicly available at github.com/salemdudeshah/skill.

In order to train intelligent systems that can seamlessly interact with their environment, they require successful training to remove background noise from audio signals. Noise interference not only hinders the performance of these systems but also degrades their safety in critical applications such as automated driving. Present-day solutions rely heavily on multi-channel audio processing techniques that aren't always feasible due to technical limitations such as the need for additional microphones. In response to this challenge, single-channel noise reduction methods have been developed but they typically suffer from oscillation issues or require extensive amounts of data for training large-scale models. To address these limitations, this paper presents a novel efficient model called the DPCRN that consists of two convolutional recurrent blocks operating in parallel, one for signal estimation and the other for error prediction. By employing this model, we achieved significant improvements in SSNR values of up to 4.3dB, 3.9dB, and 3.5dB in scenarios with heavy background noise such as speech, babble, and factory noise respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art methods including multi-channel solutions. The code for the DPCRN is available at: https://github.com/lingyu-93/DPCRN.
