The proliferation of six-degree freedom (6DOF) viewing technology opens up new possibilities for interactive and immersive 360-degree virtual tourism videos. To provide the best viewing experience, users should be directed to more engaging and significant parts of the video. This task is referred to as perspective prediction, where the predicted perspective is the optimal viewing angle within the video frame. In this paper, a novel approach is taken to forecast the user's perspective based solely on video subtitles. After incorporating semantic information from subtitles, a decision-making system is designed to determine the most relevant viewing angle. The angle's relevance is measured by the user's interaction history, and a reward function is defined to calculate the reward associated with each frame. A black-box model can be utilized for knowledge transfer to a linear model in a zero-shot setting where models share the same feature space. Although a linear model can be trained using standard linear methods, there's a knowledge gap that hinders direct application. A decision-based black-box model operates as a barrier to access its features, taking its input as a black box, making feature transfer impossible. A novel technique is introduced that extracts critical information from a black-box model by classifying it on phantom data, enabling feature transfer and subsequently linear model training. A zero-shot knowledge transfer setting is then achieved by adjusting the linear model's coefficients without retraining, leveraging the transferred knowledge. Experimental results show this technique's effectiveness across various black-box models in different scenarios. The introduced method demonstrates knowledge transfer on a cardiac segmentation task using a U-Net black-box model and in a zero-shot classification setting across multiple datasets. The technique is also analyzed to require a minimal number of model queries, allowing it to work with large-scale black-box models, and multiple ways are shown to customize the linear model for better performance. The introduced method yields results comparable to retraining the linear model with a significant reduction in computational costs, making it suitable for embedded implementations. The technique is further generalized to work with other types of black-box models, such as graph neural networks, by simply accessing their input and output. The code for the project is available at this link https://github.com/abhinav33/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer.

Understanding the efficacy of imitation learning for various tasks is crucial, however this approach often relies on an expert to provide demonstrations, which can be time consuming and expensive to obtain, especially in dynamic scenarios.  In this research, we deviate from relying on expert input and instead develop a method called Co-Imitation Training (CIT), which combines imitation learning with a comparison between the performance of two agents, including one that is more skilled.  Through comparison and imitation, the less skilled agent learns from the other and as a result, both agents become more proficient.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in multiple challenging scenarios, including scenarios with varying levels of common knowledge and scenarios where one agent has significant expertise.  Our findings show that CIT leads to both agents becoming more skilled and in many cases, one agent becomes significantly more skilled than the other.  We also explore the potential of CIT for further improvement by incorporating multiple comparing agents, as well as the potential to transition directly to reinforcement learning learning.  Our results indicate that in many cases, comparing with multiple agents that have different levels of expertise can lead to diverse learning outcomes, however this may also lead to instability in some cases, which can be alleviated through appropriate hyperparameter settings, or by incorporating multiple comparing agents gradually, as in the case of transition to reinforcement learning learning.  We believe that CIT provides a versatile method called Co-Imitation Learning (COIL) that can be used in a wide range of situations, including situations where comparing with multiple agents that have different levels of expertise may lead to unstable outcomes, as long as both agents learn from the comparison, as we demonstrate through multiple experiments.  Our research also involves a simulated scenario where comparing with multiple agents that have different levels of expertise allows us to model complex social dynamics, which can be used as a hard challenge for reinforcement learning, as well as comparing the performance of CIT with current imitation learning methods, which shows that in many cases, comparing with multiple agents that have different levels of expertise leads to better outcomes, however this may also lead to situations where both agents become less skilled, which can be alleviated through appropriate hyperparameter settings, or by incorporating multiple comparing agents gradually, as in the case of transition to reinforcement learning learning.  We believe that our research provides a solid foundation for future research, which can be used to enhance the robustness of COIL, as well as to explore the potential of comparing with multiple agents that have different levels of expertise in various situations, which can be used to model complex social dynamics,

Evaluating the best action space size for reinforcement learning-based neural machine translation remains unclear, as both discrete word-level and action-probability-based approaches have their own limitations. A rigorous exploration of action space sizes reveals that larger spaces lead to performance degradation, contrary to common assumptions. To enhance translation quality, we reduce the action space by strategically selecting next actions, resulting in a significant 1.19 glossa word improvement over the baseline in the English-French translation task, and 1.05 glossa word improvement in the English-German context. Our method also demonstrates versatility when combined with different reinforcement learning objectives and threshold-based decoding methods. Our code has been made available at https://github.com/ghru/RL-NMT-action-space.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating because non-equilibrium dynamics can often result in successful suppression of decoherence and sustained quantum operations. To investigate this, our group theoretically demonstrated a constant stream of directed heat flow could be achieved in a driven and coupled system. We proposed and implement a experimental test using a superconducting qubit coupled to a mechanical microwave cavity, driven by a periodic radiation and surrounded by pure thermal noise. Our theoretical analysis shows a specific non-equilibrium state can be stabilized, both theoretically and experimentally, which is characterized by a directed heat flow and heat current oscillations that are out of phase. We believe this system could also be applicable in the production of directed beam of ions and neutral particles. Lastly, we discuss possible extensions and modifications to the system that could lead to successful implementation in larger systems, such as lattices and directed transport systems. The creation of a directed beam of ions and neutral particles has far-reaching implications if combined with techniques of quantum simulation, as it could lead to the generation of complex, long-lived quantities of matter in the laboratory. The system's ability to maintain and sustain directed flow and current even in the presence of decoherence and spontaneous radiation emission also makes it a promising area of study that could connect to ground breaking ideas in quantum thermodynamics and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL key-value store for
data storage. In addition to its core data storage capabilities, MongoDB offers a
range of advanced features, including support for transactions, opacity, and
transactional coherence guarantees. However, the complexity of MongoDB's source
code, which spans approximately 140,000 lines of code, along with its rapid evolution
rate, presents significant challenges for manual verification of its behavior.
To address this issue, we developed an open-source formal specification of
MongoDB's core components, using the F# language, and demonstrated the correct
behavior of MongoDB's core components using the Dafny program verifier.
Furthermore, we established that MongoDB's core components satisfy transactional
coherence guarantees in isolated transactions, and also provided evidence of
satisfaction of visibility and consistency guarantees in multi-data-center deployments
of MongoDB.
Additionally, we identified an existing issue with MongoDB's data storage format,
known as "sort order," which affects the performance of various queries, including
range-based ones, and proposed a possible correction, along with associated
performance benefits.
Our formal specification of MongoDB's core components provides a foundation for
future extensions and adaptations, and our findings related to the "sort order"
issue illustrate the utility of this approach. Our research was conducted during
the course of an internship with the MongoDB company, and our results have been
discussed with the relevant development teams.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from the Solar Wind Electromagnetic Investigation suite on board the Parker Solar Probe. The probe's close approaches to the sun, within 27.8 solar radii, allowed a precise measurement of the energy flux in the solar wind. The energy flux was found to be highest in the range of 20-30 solar radii, significantly lower than expected based on mathematical models from the same range of heights. This finding can be explained by the solar wind's composition, which shows a stronger decrease with distance than predicted, mainly due to the greater loss of higher-energy particles closer to the sun. The research took into account the effects of solar wind acceleration, the energy spectrum of the particles, and the impact of the breeze on the solar wind and the energy flux, and it confirmed the results of a similar study based on models from the Ulysses and Voyager probes, with similar accuracy required to confirm the alleged solar wind slowdown in the range of 3-5 solar radii. The data from the Solar Probes' 7.5-year orbit around the sun, through the Cosmic Ray Status package, may provide further insights into the issue. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the accuracy of this research relies on properly accounting for instrumental effects that influence temperature and polarization measurements. As such, we have developed the s4cmb package to simulate instrumental biases in cosmic microwave background experiments. This package facilitates the computation of bias vectors for both temperature and polarization anisotropies, allowing for the assessment of instrumental effects on bias detection tools commonly employed in cosmic microwave background analysis. The s4cmb package supports multiple pixelation schemes, enables the simulation of complete sky maps, and incorporates pre-computed anisotropy spectra for convenience. Furthermore, we have implemented an intuitive command-line interface and an interactive Python module for easy package usage. The s4cmb package is a valuable resource for researchers working with cosmic microwave background data, particularly in identifying and mitigating instrumental biases that can impact accuracy in various analysis tasks. The code is available for public use at https://github.com/IBIS-project/s4cmb. The development of the s4cmb package was supported by the Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation at the University of Portsmouth. The authors would also like to acknowledge the financial contributions of the European Research Council and the Science and Technology Facilities Council. The s4cmb package is intended to be a starting point for further extensions and customizations, as evidenced by the presence of open issues and feature requests on its GitHub page. The validation of the package has been performed through comparative analyses of actual and simulated data from three cosmic microwave background experiments: COBE-DMR, WMAP, and Planck. The results of these validations are presented in the appendix of this document. The simulation of polarized anisotropies in the s4cmb package requires the input of $T_{\rm CMB}$, which is currently set to 2.725 based on default package settings. However, this value can be adjusted by researchers through customizations of the package. The s4cmb package comprises three primary modules: biask, biaspk, and biasp, which handle the computation of bias vectors for cosmic microwave background anisotropies based on temperature, polarization, and combined analyses, respectively. In the task of arranging words into a meaningful sentence, both human and automated systems can typically determine the correct order. While both rely on a grammar rule system and semantic knowledge, the underlying mechanisms for this process are thought to differ. This study examines the capabilities of pre-trained language models in arranging words, using BART as a representative example. Through carefully crafted tests, our findings reveal that these models primarily rely on their language generation abilities rather than a inherent understanding of the task, and that they can be fooled by adding nonsense characters to the word set. Furthermore, our analysis into the structural errors made by the model, such as inserting words into the middle of the sentence, suggests that these violations of the subject-verb-object sentence structure can be attributed to a tendency to prioritize semantic coherence over syntactic coherence. To demonstrate this, we show that simply sorting the words by their distance to the desired SVO order can significantly improve the arrangement task. This is especially evident when the input set contains multiple possible sentence structures, presenting a problem that we term structural polysemy. This research also explores possible methods to enhance BART's performance in arranging words, including utilizing multiple injection points, varying the sentence length, and testing different sentence structures, with intriguing results. Finally, our investigation into the underlying mechanics of BART highlights the complexities of understanding the internal workings of large language models, and the challenges of evaluating their simple application using simple datasets. This is reflected in the performance of BART on standard evaluation metrics, which appears lackluster compared to other state-of-the-art models. This study utilizes the word arrangement task to demonstrate the intricate nature of these models, suggesting that their simplicity has been overestimated and that much remains to be discovered about their internal mechanics. This research is applicable to a broad range of text generation tasks that involve manipulating existing texts, and provides multiple code repositories available online. Fraud schemes on the internet have historically been effective due to their simplicity and the anonymity they provide to scammers. The emergence of blockchain technology offers a new level of transparency, making it more challenging for conspiratorial fraud schemes to operate and succeed. This research examines the intricate structure of a successful play-to-earn game scam called "Forsage," which used smart contracts and a pyramid-based compensation plan to defraud at least $25 million from over 250,000 victims. Through a detailed analysis of the scheme's code and operational aspects, we reveal the elaborate techniques used by the scammers to maintain their anonymity, evade detection, and exploit vulnerabilities in the Ethereum platform and various cryptocurrency exchanges. Our findings highlight the difficulties Forsage's administrators overcame in creating and maintaining the scheme, as well as the ways in which it was designed to avoid detection and criticism. We also examine the financial and statistical aspects of the scheme and provide a comprehensive breakdown of its code. Our data suggests that Forsage was an exceptional instance of a game scam, capable of paying out substantial dividends to its participants due to its unique design, which allowed it to generate $10 million per month in operating surpluses. We believe that sharing Forsage's code, financial data, and operational analysis will be beneficial to researchers, developers, and various industry stakeholders, and may help prevent similar scams from occurring in the future. This research was conducted in accordance with Ethereum's ethical guidelines, in collaboration with the blockchain analytics firm, Chainalysis, and with the permission of the relevant law enforcement agencies. We have taken extensive precautions to ensure that the victims' identities remain anonymous. The code and financial data associated with Forsage have been made public, and can be accessed through the MIT License. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. In this research, we develop an innovative clustering method called Impact Based Clustering (IBC) to analyze complex systems whose behavior changes over time. We classify systems into different categories based on how their dynamics respond to events, such as whether they move towards each other, stay the same, or move apart. We then use clustering to group systems into these categories. However, the process of achieving this IBC structure is challenging because it involves determining when events occur and how systems respond to them. To overcome this obstacle, we rely on short-time observations of systems. From these observations, we identify events and assess the system's response to them. We can then use clustering to group systems based on their response to these events. Unlike traditional methods, IBC detects events automatically and doesn't require knowledge of the system's dynamics. Instead, it uses the data itself to determine when events happen and how systems respond to them. We validate IBC on mathematical models and real-world data, including time series related to economics and sports. The results show that IBC effectively detects events and accurately describes the system's response to them. Furthermore, we find that IBC yields meaningful insights that other methods miss. These issues are particularly apparent in data related to sports. With IBC, we can now incorporate these random changes and time-dependent dynamics into our analysis. We can do this by treating the system's response to events as a time-varying probability distribution. To achieve this, we develop an innovative method called Time-Varying Markov Clustering (TVMC). In recent years, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have gained significant ground in natural language processing tasks like text generation. However, achieving optimal performance from these models is challenging due to the difficulty in balancing training stability and generating diversity. We introduce SparseGAN, a novel GAN architecture that overcomes this limitation by incorporating a new adversary module specifically designed to produce a compact representation of discriminative information. We further develop a novel training technique that uses a combination of maximum likelihood estimation and a latent adversary loss to produce more coherent and diverse generated text. Our proposed architecture and training method are collectively responsible for a range of benefits, including improved coherence and reduced mode collapse. Interestingly, we also observe that this model can be effectively applied for text classification, where it employs the adversary module to focus on essential classification features, resulting in elevated performance compared to existing GAN-based approaches. Our evaluation utilities a range of text generation datasets, including the commonly used WikiText-2 and CLOTH, along with available classification datasets listed in the paper. Our results demonstrate sparseGAN's superior performance in terms of coherence and diversity for text generation, along with enhanced performance in various text classification setups. Our code has been made publicly available for public use.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a method was developed to predict the fate of microbial life forms that could have been carried on a space rock, taking into account various factors such as radiation, temperature, and the presence of a host star's gravitational influence as it interacts with a planetary system. By utilizing this approach, researchers examined various scenarios to determine if it would be possible to identify signs of interstellar panspermia, perhaps even with current capabilities, by analyzing the conditions on comets or in the vicinity of exoplanetary systems. In particular, a study found that it may be feasible to detect evidence of interstellar microorganisms on Kepler-452b, a famous exoplanet often referred to as "Earth's twin". Although this result is intriguing, more computational power is needed to fully explore this finding in depth. In addition, other exoplanetary systems, including K2-141b and HAT-P-11b, also presented promising outcomes, while comets like 67P/Churyumov-Geyserat and Borrelly showed that it may be difficult to detect preserved microorganisms on certain types of comets. In general, detecting the remains of interstellar microorganisms on a planet or comet is unlikely to be straightforward, but it is unlikely to be extremely challenging, and there are various simplifications that can be made to the analysis that may make it more feasible. In the course of this research, a related concept known as stellar symbiosis also emerged, which could potentially be discovered by looking for pairs of planets orbiting the same star showing signs of life on different masses, or by searching for microorganisms on comets that could have originated from the same solar system as the stars with which they are interacting, thus revealing the extent of those systems' capabilities for supporting life. Although there are numerous compelling outcomes from this study, more computational power and larger datasets are needed to fully explore the possibilities of interstellar panspermia, and thus a new code has been developed that can handle these issues and can be used for other similar research projects in the future.

Animal population studies often rely on capture-recapture data, both on the same site where animals make choices based on resource availability, and in different locations where animals move between them. This study extends previous research by combining capture-recapture data from varied locations, incorporating information about how animals select sites based on the availability of resources, in order to estimate the distribution of a population. A new Bayesian method is proposed to achieve this goal. The proposed method involves modeling capture-recapture data from each site using capture probability, modeling site choice using a logit regression with random effects, and estimating the density of the population using capture probability and capture probability density, all while accounting for detection bias. The performance of the new method is evaluated through simulations. The proposed method and a related reference method are compared by applying them to real capture-recapture data from sites with resource choice, and the results are analyzed. The new method demonstrates the importance of considering detection random effects, facilitates inference about the distribution of the population, and provides a way to evaluate the quality of the sites for further studies. The proposed approach can be expanded to multi-season studies, and the challenges of extending it to this level are discussed. The new method, combined with knowledge of species ecology, can contribute to managing populations and identifying areas with high conservation value. This new model provides a more accurate representation of certain dynamic systems than traditional single-layer models. Furthermore, we have investigated the transmission of solutions in multilayer networks with layer overlap, discovering that the transmission of signals between oscillators in different layers can result in the creation of new isolated components and affect the stability of the system. Our research has implications for a range of fields, including neuroscience, economics, and climate science, where the importance of signal transmission between different components is well documented. We have also made our results available in the form of an interactive dashboard that enables users to explore our findings graphically. This study can serve as a foundation for future investigations into the complex dynamics of multilayer networks. Our code is available for download upon request. The methodology used in this study is applicable to a wide range of multilayer network models, including those with directed connections and weighted edges. Finally, we have identified potential future research avenues in this area. To address this limitation, our study investigated healthy young adults walking on a treadmill to establish a foundation for comparison. We analyzed ECoG signals captured from the motor cortices to accurately predict subjects' walking states and their corresponding step rates. By utilizing a machine learning-based model, our results showed significant accuracy in predicting step rates and walking states, respectively. We observed a positive correlation between predicted step rates and actual step rates in healthy individuals. Furthermore, our data revealed distinct neural representations of step rates, and we found that the predicted walking states could be accurately determined based on the integration of predicted step rates over time. Our findings from this study can be utilized as a baseline to decode the walking state and step rate from ECoG signals, and may also serve valuable purposes in understanding the neural mechanisms underlying human movement. We believe that further exploration of these mechanisms will provide valuable insights for the development of effective neuroprosthetic limbs. In addition, our research illustrates that walking state and step rate can be reconstructed from ECoG signals, and we have made the necessary code available on GitHub for public access. Finally, our findings related to the correlation between the predicted step rates and actual step rates, and the neural representations of step rates, among other results, are significant and valuable contributions of our study. We have also investigated the effects of different parameter variations on the accuracy of our BCI, and our results show that the performance of the BCI remains robust across different parameter settings. Our study used healthy individuals walking on treadmills, and our results compared the associated ECoG signals with those obtained from previous studies related to walking in individuals with specific neurological disorders. Our data analysis consisted of six individual experiments, and we analyzed the results of each experiment in detail. We investigate right-angled Artin complexes based on finite graphs and show that any nonpositive curvature condition loses at least one essential feature when moved from the underlying graph. Specifically, if a graph supports a negatively curved complex, it must be a tree, providing a curved complex that is minimally sensitive to small changes. Additionally, we find that there is no equivalent to the mean curvature property for left-angled Artin complexes based on non-tree graphs. However, for general right-angled Artin complexes based on finite graphs, we obtain an inductive formula that reconstructs a curved complex from its subcomplexes and associated graph components. This inductive approach also works for left-angled Artin complexes based on finite graphs, providing a new proof of the fact that they cannot have negative curvature. Our results further generalize to various generalized Artin groups. Moreover, our inductive formula is applicable to combinations of these groups and generalizations, including both left and right versions. Finally, our research involves exploring the relationship between a group's geometric properties and those of the underlying graph, providing a new proof of the fact that a finite graph is a tree if it supports a quasihyperbolic metric with finite diameter. This in turn leads to the conclusion that there are curves that cannot be expressed as the geodesics in a curved complex based on that graph. Identifying the connections between interrelated time series data can lead to a deeper understanding of complex systems and may reveal connections between different components, potentially revealing a system's modular structure. While connectivity estimation techniques can achieve this, they typically require static, rather than dynamic, data and are typically based on correlation, although correlations may not necessarily imply directed connections. Furthermore, modeling the underlying connections and using the estimated connections in downstream tasks in a, thus far, automated manner remains challenging. In response to these difficulties, we introduce a method called Deep Dynamic Connectivity Estimation, in which directed connections between time series are modeled as switching between different states, and which provides a, thus far, automated prediction of downstream task performance using the estimated connections. We demonstrate that our method is capable of accurately predicting downstream task performance and identifies the optimal number of dynamic states and timing of variation in data through new metrics such as the time-dependent connectivity matrix prediction error and the connectivity transition probability. When applied to downstream tasks, our method's performance is comparable to that of similar methods that utilize the same data, although with much fewer parameters. We also show that our method's performance can be varied through hyperparameters such as the number of dynamic states and timing of variation in data through controlled experiments. Furthermore, we provide code and trained models for reproducibility and demonstrate that our method's performance extends to difficult problems such as immunology through collaboration with subject matter experts. Last, we show that our method's performance can be improved through the use of related time series data such as genomic data in the difficult problem of identifying connections between components of a complex system. We believe that our method, for which all code is available at https://github.com/alberto1333/Deep_Dynamic_CTE, can be applied to a wide range of problems involving the analysis of complex systems through the analysis of time series data. Last, we propose a new theorem regarding dynamic connectivity and provide a mathematical proof of the theorem. Last, we show that our method is capable of modeling a type of dynamic connectivity known as the loopy process, for which there is a mathematical representation available. Last, we demonstrate that our method is capable of estimating connections from a special type of time series known as multivariate Bernoulli processes, for which there is a mathematical representation available. Last, we propose a new metric for evaluating the transition probability of dynamic connectivity and provide a mathematical explanation of the metric. Last, we propose a new metric for evaluating the connectivity matrix prediction error of dynamic connectivity and provide a mathematical explanation of the metric.

Animals play a significant part in conveying fundamental biological principles to students through real-world examples.  Moving organisms can be found in various settings, including forests, oceans, and even within themselves, presenting different levels of complexity.  Videos showcasing these movements are readily available, offering a valuable educational tool.  However, pinpointing the most relevant sections of an video can be time-consuming and inconsistent in quality.  To address this challenge, we outline a computational method for automatically identifying the most significant parts of a video featuring a moving organism.  This approach involves assessing the importance of each frame based on its association with the overall structure of the biologic entity in question.  We demonstrate this approach using videos featurting trees, plants, forests, and organisms including ants, bees, and birds.  In doing so we provide a straightforward means for generating a score for each frame, as well as a more sophisticated metric that compares the overall structure of the biologic entity across different videos.  We also discuss the potential applications of this method in contexts beyond education, such as in conservation biology.  The code for this project is available at https://github.com/0XXX/BioVideo.  We show that a simple and a complex approach to evaluating the significance of each frame yield nearly identical results.  In addition to identifying the most significant parts of a video we also provide a means of comparing the overall structure of a biologic entity across different videos including trees, plants, forests, ants, bees, and birds.  This method can be used in a variety of settings including education and conservation biology.  We offer this method as a tool for detecting movement in videos of static objects or scenes. Researchers explored topological Anderson conductors with spatially correlated and changing electric disorders in a 3D cubic network.  They discovered topological properties in these conductors, as indicated by a gap in their spectral spectra, occurred in all previously undefined patterns of correlated disorders.  Additionally, they found that the width of the energy gap around a central value, varied significantly with the strength of the correlated disorders, even when the disorders were randomly distributed.  The opening of the energy gap was found to be directly related to the presence of a topological phase, as was the formation of a pair of narrow energy bands on either side of the energy gap, which could be influenced by the correlated disorders or random distribution of disorders.  The occurrence of a energy gap was shown to be a reliable indicator of the topological properties of a material, allowing it to be detected in 3D networks using experimental methods such as photoemission spectroscopy.  The theoretical understanding of these findings was combined with experimental results showing that complex materials made with carbon and nitrogen-based molecules, and packed with metal and semiconductor particles, exhibit both topological and periodic energy gap properties.  The predicted effects of changing electric disorders on these materials were also detected in experimental results, using methods such as scanning tunneling microscopy, resonance photoemission spectroscopy, and X-ray fluorescence. Specifically, $C$ remains unchanged under rotations, inversion, and translation of the input disc, as well as the corresponding actions on the function $f$. Our study investigates outcomes of the event shape manipulation method recently introduced by B. Schenke et al. The approach aims to disentangle flow from fragmentationality in Pb-Pb collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy. The event shape manipulation method splits events into four categories based on the centrality of the most and least peripheral events considered. We compare the second-order flow coefficient ($v_2$) for different event shape manipulations and find that its value remains largely unaffected. In contrast, the $v_2$ coefficient exhibits a significant change when analyzing the inclusive $v_2$ distribution of charged particles. The results hold true for different particle species and become more pronounced for particles with higher momentum. The findings are consistent with theoretical predictions suggesting that the event shape manipulation method can influence inclusive $v_2$ distributions due to their sensitivity to the radial flow component. Nonetheless, the relative insensitivity of $v_2$ to event shape manipulations also makes it possible to study radial flow in experiments. The research was conducted using the AMPT model and ALICE collision data. The study delves into the underlying mechanics and provides numerical evidence within the AMPT model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the event shape manipulation method can be effectively applied to extract elliptic flow coefficients from the ALICE collision data. The resulting $v_2$ distributions are compatible with the hydrodynamic model proposed by the PH-QM collaboration. The research yields unique insights into the event shape manipulation method and radial flow components in heavy-ion physics. This work investigates the extremal values of the gain from optimal power control in interference networks and obtains two main results. Firstly, we establish an upper bound on the extremal gain from power control, demonstrating that this gain cannot exceed the square root of $K$ when considering the greatest gain in a network with $K$ users. Secondly, we show that this upper bound is achievable and thus holds as a lower bound, specifically in a specific scenario with $K$ users where all users except one have binary power control. This lower bound can be interpreted as a lower bound on the extremal gain from power control to one user when the remaining users have binary power control. Furthermore, we establish that this lower bound is viable in the limit as the number of users with binary power control grows without bound, thus it holds for a network with an arbitrary large number of users with binary power control. This growth without bound can be quantified as $\sqrt{K}$ in a Generalized Degrees of Freedom analysis. This growth without bound is validated for both the gain from power control to one user and the gain from power control to all users. This gain without bound is also expressed as a lower bound on the extremal gain from power control to one user when the remaining users have nearly optimal power control, which can be quantified as $\sqrt{K}$ in a Generalized Degrees of Freedom analysis. Validation of this method has been performed by comparing it with existing approaches and evaluating its performance in simulations of single collision events, particle interactions, and flow interactions between particles and wall boundaries. For the integer expression $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, we derive a bounding statement that demonstrates an significant improvement over existing results, specifically for values of $n$ exceeding $703$. Moreover, this binding statement indirectly supports the unproved conjecture of Albert and Lewis, which asserts that all positive integers forming the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ must be powers of a specific prime number, in this case $7$. In addition, we explore two specific cases where one or both of the integers $a$ and $b$ are set to $7$, which allows us to establish additional solution sets. Finally, we outline an strategy for extending our findings to the original Albert and Lewis conjecture, which remains an open problem. This research focuses on advancing the design of a monopod for hopping on soft, uneven ground by conducting simulations and improving the initial design. The aim is to explore the feasibility of a monopod for hazardous terrains considered off-limits for traditional four-legged robots. The soft environment was simulated using a finite element method, and the impact on the ground was assessed using a factor critical to ensuring safety around human assets. To enhance the design, modifications were made, and these changes were validated through physical experiments. The monopod's hopping pattern was also altered to minimize the impact radius, and a successful reduction of 45% in the area affected was demonstrated. Furthermore, a control strategy was developed to accommodate unexpected soft ground, resulting in a successful hike through a scenario mimicking such conditions. The system's versatility was proven by transferring the design to a different terrain and successfully adapting to it. This implies that the operators in question are surjective when restricted to $\Omega$. This result holds without requiring compactness of the boundary of $\Omega$ or relying on assumptions about the nature of $X$ and its topology. This means that the operators in question are surjective when restricted to $\Omega$ in this case as well. This result can be generalized to hold for differential operators of any order. Ten years ago, at the inaugural Formal Proof Day, I described an idea for creating a versatile format to express proofs linking SAT and decision procedures, which I termed the SAT Proof Format (SPF). Since then, SPF has undergone significant evolution, incorporating valuable feedback and new concepts. At the tenth anniversary of that event, I'm pleased to present an expanded version of SPF, which we now call the Basic Proof Format (BPF). BPF builds upon the principles of its predecessor by providing a simple, SAT-based proof format that enables the verification of conjectures using a variety of theories beyond the original SAT solver proof style. It supports the integration of multiple reasoning systems, each employing its own distinct proof style. BPF has been implemented in the Alethe proof assistant, which is designed to streamline the process of verifying the correctness of algorithms and deciding properties of formulas by providing an efficient way to convert conjectures to a form that can be verified using BPF. This version of BPF further refines the proof style of SAT to include ordered pairs in a way that extends naturally to higher-arithmetic proofs. This extension has been implemented in the context of integer and rational arithmetic, which are now available in Alethe. Moreover, we present a simple and intuitive syntax for expressing the BPF, along with a parser that can be used to create new solvers and a command-line interface for verifying conjectures and interacting with the Alethe system. The underlying principles and architecture of BPF are discussed in depth, along with the implementation of the Alethe system and the pair-based proof style. The talk will also address some of the challenges we encountered and the various ways in which we were able to overcome them. Finally, we conclude by examining some possible future extensions to the BPF, including ways to enhance the proof style, the implementation of real numbers, and the integration of first-order logic. The slides for this talk are available at the URL given below. I welcome any feedback from the audience. The URL is https://www.alethe.io/talks/2023-06-20_bpf.html. I look forward to your questions and any feedback you may have. Thank you.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling devices with rare connections to contribute to learning. This method, which allows gradient updates without restriction, results adaptive learning rates that cater to individual devices. By ascribing distinct meanings to the gradient and update vectors, researchers have established that FedBuff yields a nearly optimal solution within a specified number of communication rounds, surpassing the performance of conventional federated learning systems by a factor dependent on the number and frequency of connecting devices. This achievement comes without the need for expensive centralized data, ensuring the validity of this finding in various settings. Furthermore, FedBuff's framework accommodates various incentive systems and Incentive-Ready FedBuff, a variant specifically designed for strategies based on weighted averages. This research also presents theoretical and practical evidence demonstrating that allowing unrestricted gradient updates is conducive to revitalizing dormant devices. Unrestricted gradient updates are made possible by assuming that the distribution of device frequencies follows a bounded logarithmic distribution, a hypothesis that is validated through real-world data obtained from multiple datasets. This discovery's limited scope provides an opportunity to extend further the already promising FedBuff framework. The code for FedBuff is available at https://github.com/ShuaiGeng/FedBuff.

When there's insufficient data for the less fluent language, this method leads to a further advancement when the more fluent language has some data available, as it establishes a solid foundation for speech recognition in this situation. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating through unfamiliar environments.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to a real-world marine robot guidance problem.  Our code is available at https://github.com/sparse-gp/spgp-td.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of domain adaptation under few shot learning conditions. This paper leverages the meta-learning framework to enhance teacher models for GEC across multiple domains with limited pair examples. The proposed method, evaluated on the NGLD dataset, demonstrates significant improvements in target domain performance compared to standard multi-task learning, with results showing that for 5-shot learning, the CV score increases by 1.3 compared to the baseline, and for 10-shot learning, the score increases by 2.3. Additionally, the research reveals that models trained on a single source domain using the proposed method can handle up to 5000 new target domains with a certain level of performance, surpassing the baseline by a 5.3 CV score margin. Moreover, the research finds that GEC tasks differ significantly from standard meta-learning challenges, with tasks often being highly similar, which is reflected in the high domain similarity score of 73.8% calculated using the proposed domain similarity metric. Finally, the research demonstrates that models trained on the proposed framework with a single source domain with a domain similarity score higher than 60% can handle over 90% of the target domains with a 10 shot setting, demonstrating a promising way to tackle the challenge with a small number of pair examples. The code for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Simple-GEC.

We are interested in identifying pure Nash equilibria in mechanisms that fairly allocate goods according to their social welfare significance. We demonstrate the existence of efficient mechanisms with relatively modest requirements for value bounds that are also guaranteed to have pure Nash equilibria. Additionally, we determine that mechanisms requiring a value bound that is a multiple of one delta (a minimal positive value an agent could potentially hold) are necessary to ensure pure Nash equilibria in this model. Furthermore, we outline a general approach for constructing equilibrious states and provide a specific explicit example of a fair mechanism with a pure Nash equilibrium for a specific number of agents. We also discuss the relationship between this model and a related model where agents' values can be accurately determined, and examine various special cases such as large agent populations and certain geometric value distributions. We complement our results by proving that certain general fair allocation criteria cannot be achieved through pure Nash equilibria in this model, and also provide an explicit example of a mechanism that achieves one of these criteria but is not efficient or fair. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline
multi-agent reinforcement learning presents a significant challenge. Since the
interaction between agents is often complex and interconnected, it's difficult
to create a reliable training set that covers all possible interactions and
scenarios. Existing methods typically rely on a uniform approach to process
data, which can result in the model's performance suffering due to the presence
of poorly labeled data. In response to this difficulty, we propose a novel
approach, named Learning from Good Paths (LGP), that focuses on processing only
the more common favorable trajectories found in the existing dataset. By using
a policy-based method, LGP establishes a more robust model that excels at
replicating these desirable behaviors. To validate the effectiveness of our
approach, we compared LGP with multiple baseline methods in two diverse scenarios,
including both small and large-scale offline multi-agent scenarios. The results
show that LGP consistently delivers superior performance compared to the existing
state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, we discovered that LGP's capacity to analyze
the interaction between agents and identify critical good trajectories is critical
to its success. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that LGP is a versatile
method that can be applied across a wide range of offline multi-agent scenarios.

The notion of single-particle entanglement is often misinterpreted, as it's not always clear why entangled particles are considered nonlocally connected. To address this, we examine single-particle entanglement's genuinely nonlocal effect – namely, the ability to remotely influence the particle's quantum state without physical contact. We argue that, in a qubit system, single-particle entanglement enables directional control over the particle's quantum state, a capability known as mechanical steering. We further demonstrate that single-particle entanglement enables a user to deliberately distribute their own entanglement with the particle, effectively establishing a nonlocal entanglement network. We also explore single-particle entanglement's equivalence to the Wigner function's nonvanishment and correlate it with mechanical steering and entanglement distribution. By analyzing these connections, we demonstrate that single-particle entanglement is a versatile and nuanced concept with various nonlocal implications. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of single-particle entanglement in nonlocal entanglement distribution and quantum communication networks. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Numerical evaluation confirms the advantages of this method, particularly in terms of data transfer reduction and system performance improvement over traditional approaches in moderate to fast fading environments. Furthermore, the proposed method's efficacy across various GMM sizes and mobile terminal precoder resolution has been assessed, demonstrating its robustness in a variety of scenarios. Most massive stars end their lives. A significant portion dies in massive supernovae explosions, while the remainder collapses into massive compact objects like black holes or neutron stars. Research suggests that certain compact objects are paired with giant stars that have massive hydrogen and helium at their cores. These stars, known as $\gamma$-ray binaries, endure high-energy radiation while undergoing a gradual death. In the course of this death, they slowly accrete material and build up mass around themselves. Eventually, this accumulation causes a massive explosion that shines brightly in the form of a giant explosion seen in the gamma-ray spectrum. The rate at which these binaries form and lose mass is unknown, as is the rate at which they lose mass and form compact objects. However, researchers were able to determine the limit for this rate of mass loss by considering the time it takes for a binary to explode and the maximum distance between these binaries and the sun. Furthermore, a new approach based on the study of the PS1-$\gamma$-ray binary distribution allows for an estimate of the mass loss rate. Specifically, it allows for an estimate of the minimum and maximum mass loss rates for the known binaries. The results from both approaches indicate that the maximum mass loss rate cannot be greater than 1.7 times 10 to the 28th power per second. The most notable of these results includes the estimation of the minimum and maximum mass loss rates for the known binaries PS1-10Fg, PS1-12Fb, and M31F-20130530. The addition of PS1-10Fg and PS1-12Fb to the established $\gamma$-ray binary pairs suggests that the mass loss rate for these binaries cannot be greater than 2.3 times 10 to the 28th power per second. The results also indicate that the minimum mass loss rate for the established binary pairs 4U 1655-40 and MWC 656 is 1.2 times 10 to the 28th power per second and 0.5 times 10 to the 28th power per second respectively. The estimation of the mass loss rate for M31F-20130530 is subject to change as the distance to the galaxy Andromeda is not well known. The results provide valuable information on the mass loss rate for the $\gamma$-ray binaries and offer insights into how these binaries form and the characteristics of the compact objects within them. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate the effectiveness of our enhancements, we conducted a straightforward evaluation of text-based search tasks within TextWorldExpress. 
Our findings showed that by incorporating our speed measurements into their reinforcement learning algorithm, agent performance could be accurately predicted, and that the majority of recorded world records would take less than a week to break under our simulation. 
All text-based game developers can benefit from our open-source optimization techniques, which are available through GitHub. 
TextWorldExpress is also suited for high-performance computing environments, offering considerable potential for further speed increases. 
In addition to text-based games, our optimization technique is relevant to any Markov decision process project involving slow simulation environments. 
Our research was presented at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing 2020. 
The current version of TextWorldExpress includes challenges derived from the DeepMind Lab text-based interface, the Malmo Unix Terminal, and the VizDoom chat. 
Our research received funding from the National Science Foundation, the Office of Naval Research, the Army Research Laboratory, and the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent approach based on Dauge's elements for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our method, the proposed approach also enables the enforcement of no-flow boundaries through blocking fractures. This is made possible by rewriting the problem using fractural edge elements and a transformation technique. Our numerical data demonstrates that this method is viable and produces accurate outcomes for a range of scenarios involving complex geometry. This approach is also shown to be comparable to other state-of-the-art methods for certain examples. Our algorithm is then applied to a real-world case study involving geothermal reservoir exploration. This study involves flow within a fractural media where the orientation of fractures significantly affects the outcome, and is modeled using blocking fractures. The resulting numerical results are also validated through comparison with analytical solutions presented in existing literature. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence ranking for machine reading comprehension, our method, called DiscSense, automatically detects these indicators between sentences and determines their semantic relationship, including their potential lack of connection. We developed two versions of DiscSense: a rule-based approach for limited indicators and a machine learning model for a broader range of discourse markers. Our technique was incorporated into a sentence ranking system, leading to improvements in performance on four different datasets, particularly in cases where the connection between sentences is minimal or non-existent. Our findings suggest that detecting discourse indicators and capturing their diverse meanings can enhance the accuracy of machine comprehension by allowing for the exclusion of unnecessarily connected sentences. The code for DiscSense is available at https://github.com/nyuvlab/DiscSense.

In an earlier paper, it was claimed that a graph needed a specific number of these edge colors, but no proof was provided. Now, we have discovered a counterexample which shows that this number is actually too high. Specifically, we have found that the graph known as Sh81-5 doesn't require the predicted number of edge colors, and by examining its structure, we can also generalize this finding to show that a particular type of complex graph, namely a cubic bipartite graph, is consistently overconservatively estimated in this edge coloring context. This achievement also gives a new answer to another unresolved problem related to a famous conjecture made by Erdos, Nielsen, and Schelp. This method involves an innovative cluster-consistent embedding framework, initially applied to generate separate embeddings for each language, and a unified framework for integrated multi-lingual embedding construction. We employ a combination of network architecture and optimization techniques to ensure that the embedding of the same semantic category crosses linguistic boundaries, thus facilitating a range of multi-lingual applications such as neural machine translation, multi-lingual document classification, and cross-lingual sentiment analysis. Our proposed approach outperforms existing multi-lingual embedding methods in multiple evaluation metrics across five different evaluation tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method's ability to construct robust semantic areas can be enhanced by incorporating additional linguistic resources, namely part-of-speech tags. Mobile agents require accurate localization, and while VIO can accomplish this, it struggles with grid size and computational expense under limited resources. This issue is exacerbated in Visual-inertial odometry (VIO), which without a prior, must estimate both states and the motion matrix, resulting in VIO outperforming VI on off-grid accuracy but at a significant computational cost. To address this limitation, a novel external memory attention model is proposed for VIO, allowing for the incorporation of prior knowledge within the map, and demonstrating significant improvements in both grid size and computational expense in comparison to standard VIO. Furthermore, with the introduction of an adaptive time-step filter, this model's accuracy is preserved even in challenging situations characterized by rapid motion. The proposed method, evaluated using a raw VIO stream from a moving vehicle, showcases the significance of modeling noise within the SEM framework, and across multiple datasets, significantly outperforms both VI and standard VIO in various scenarios, including indoor and outdoor settings. The proposed method, entitled EMA-VIO, also demonstrates a high level of compatibility with change-detecting models, enabling it to adjust its map effectively. The code for EMA-VIO is available at this link: https://github.com/yh-95/EMA-VIO.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is tailored to contribute to the ongoing discussion within the scientific community as part of the Venus Express 11th Scientific Conference.

A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to evaluating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, focusing on the strength and timing of cross-event connections. This methodical analysis of the model's properties has revealed that its performance is comparable to traditional estimation methods, with Bayesian methods successfully identifying the presence of dormant connections, which can be fragile, even with moderate rates of events. Furthermore, we have applied this nonparametric Bayesian framework to estimate the parameters of a nonlinear Hawkes process from synthetic data generated by an algebraic nonlinear Hawkes process, and also from real-world datasets, including earthquake magnitudes and online message streams. This analysis has provided insights into the performance of this model on such datasets, with complex graph-based variants demonstrating promising performance. This format can be utilized for the development of X-ray cameras for a next-generation hard X-ray telescope focusing on wide-field observations. Furthermore, this layout enables us to assess the effectiveness of lobster-eye optics in a more realistic scenario, providing insights that can be applied to a variety of astronomical and non-astronomical applications. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time identification required for multi-messenger astronomy. We detail a deep learning platform developed in-house, entitled "Wildest," through which these findings were achieved. Wildest enables various deep learning approaches including all convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and hybrid models, facilitating both individual and combined performances. We also explore various network modifications and alternatives that enhance the results, and demonstrate the potential of transfer learning to train highly complex models on limited data. Ultimately, these outcomes provide a foundation for identifying future neutron star and binary neutron star mergers detected by LIGO, and offer a framework for adapting to future detectors and other electromagnetic facilities. We discuss the potential of these models on current and upcoming detectors including the upgraded LIGO and the Virgo detector, and analyze the predicted detection rates for future detectors expected to detect mergers at much weaker signal levels. We conclude by examining the scope for improving these results and exploring related problems, including the reconstruction of event parameters and the prediction of electromagnetic radiation. We anticipate that the findings presented here will contribute to the successful implementation of real-time gravitational wave analysis for the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo, and facilitate multi-messenger astronomy in the decades to come. The code used in this study is available at https://github.com/gw-poc.

This could occur when the economic effects outweigh the societal benefits of restricting interactions, leading to increased mobility among higher-income individuals and decreased mobility among lower-income individuals. The massive protostars, with masses over 30 times that of our sun, are likely formed through the collapse of dense gas clouds. However, unlike lower-mass protostars, massive protostars experience significant pressure forces due to the substantial surrounding gas and particles, which restrict their ability to shine with the typical stellar temperature. Research suggests that the surrounding environments of massive protostars are dense and highly turbulent, indicating that their formation might be influenced by external factors, but the specific process remains unknown. New observations made using the APEX 870 $\mu$m submillimeter plate sensitivity detector, combined with existing data from radio and infrared observatories, reveal that the most massive protostars are often located in groups that are interacting with their surrounding environments, suggesting that these protostars may have formed through the collision of dense gas clouds. This theory is supported by the discovery of two protostars that are connected by an ridge of falling gas, indicating that the surrounding environments play a significant role in forming massive protostars. If this process is common, it would explain the formation of the most massive stars, as well as the creation of binary star systems where the components have similar masses. Furthermore, it may also contribute to the formation of dense star clusters that contain massive young stars, as well as the creation of molecular ridges that are associated with gas clouds collapsing under their own gravity. If this is the case, then the term "isolated" might not be suitable for some of the massive protostars studied here. The collaboration recommends utilizing more sensitive detectors with higher spatial resolution in future observations, which could reveal more detailed information about the formation of massive protostars and provide insights into the specific processes that form the most massive stars, the binary star systems with similar mass components, the dense star clusters that contain massive young stars, as well as the molecular ridges that are associated with gas clouds collapsing under their own gravity. We focus on the situation where the mean flow speed is sufficiently slow that the circulation remains steady and the statistical properties of the interface modulation can be described using a Hamiltonian Hamilton-Dysthe equation from the full water wave system. By comparing the Hamilton-Dysthe equation with the actual water wave system, we determine the relevant parameters that must be large or small for the Hamilton-Dysthe equation to accurately represent the interface modulation, and demonstrate that the Hamilton-Dysthe equation can be a good model even when the circulation is not extremely large. Additionally, we identify specific instances where the Hamilton-Dysthe equation fails to predict the interface modulation accurately. Furthermore, we solve the Hamilton-Dysthe equation in the cases of weak nonlinearities and constant circulation, and show that the results align with existing knowledge. Lastly, we analyze the constant circulation case in more detail, and demonstrate that the interface modulation can be effectively characterized using a scalar Hamilton-Dysthe equation, a fact that we demonstrate by solving this equation numerically and comparing the results to the original water wave system. Lastly, we investigate the situation where the initial interface modulation is randomly selected, and show that the Hamilton-Dysthe equation predicts that the circulation will become unstable in a finite time, although we note that this predicted instability time can be quite long, potentially exceeding the timescale of the system by several orders of magnitude. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in the underlying architecture, as well as paths forward for future research in the field. The code is available at https://github.com/AhmedHamdy267/CMTR-BERT.
