Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, as large models like BERT have become prevalent, their pre-trained capability has enabled them to draw inferences without relying on annotated data. In this work, we focus on emotion-related question annotation and experiment with BERT to derive insights. We discovered that BERT can accurately determine annotation mistakes by comparing the predicted labels of emulated models including BERT, in conjunction with labeled data, against standard annotation guidelines. To demonstrate this, we developed a tool that leverages BERT to identify potentially erroneous annotations by matching them to labeled data generated by models including BERT. We evaluated this tool on annotated data related to emotions and discovered that BERT's expertise can be used to enhance the accuracy of annotation by approximately 14% in search annotation and 10% in selection annotation. We also found that BERT's proficiency in addressing annotation mistakes holds up even when considering a more conservative standard of correction, as well as when evaluating only the most contentious examples. In addition, we observed that BERT's capability to correct annotations is comparable to adding 100 extra labeled data samples, a quantity that is particularly significant where labeled data is scarce. Nonetheless, we acknowledge limitations with the current approach, specifically the difficulty of incorporating intuitive annotation guidelines that go beyond simple classification. In conclusion, using BERT to correct annotation mistakes offers a promising and straightforward strategy with applications across the machine learning lifecycle, from data preparation to model validation. In the process of conducting this research, we released an open-source tool called BERT-Annotate, which is available for public use. Moreover, we released a new dataset containing the annotated text for 15 emotion-related question-answering templates, in addition to 5 simple templates for which BERT failed in annotation correction. We believe this newly created dataset, along with BERT-Annotate, can serve as a valuable resource for developing more sophisticated models, including but not limited to BERT and its variants. We also released a related technical report that includes additional details about BERT-Annotate, along with guidelines and statistics regarding the annotation correction task. Lastly, we welcomed interested researchers to join us in further enhancing BERT-Annotate and exploring new possibilities with annotation correction. We currently offer BERT-Annotate as a standalone tool available for download, in addition to providing installation instructions on our website. Furthermore, we released a related technical report that includes additional details about BERT-Annotate, along with guidelines and statistics regarding the annotation correction task.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings, having an effective mapping technique is crucial. In this research, we introduce HiTMap, a novel navigation map format featuring interconnected circular modules, and we demonstrate the efficacy of this representation in particular, consisting of triangular sub-modules within its circular components. We have conducted comprehensive simulations to evaluate the performance of HiTMap, mapping it against an advanced text-based representation known as Topological Map (ToM). Our findings, set against a backdrop of constantly evolving environments and limited sensor capabilities, reveal that HiTMap exhibits a significant advantage over ToM, yielding a 25% improvement in mapping accuracy and a 15% gain in navigation efficiency. Furthermore, our results show that HiTMap offers a 20% decrease in memory utilization compared to ToM. Our research in this paper is concluded by outlining potential enhancements to HiTMap, including the integration of spatial attributes within its circular and triangular modules, which could contribute to an even more precise localization through increased spatial awareness. These integrated modules could take the form of HiTMap's current triangular modules, where landmarks are represented as positive values, and obstacles are represented as negative values, with the default value set at zero, representing free space. This study investigates finite mixture models through the lens of stochastic convex geometry. We demonstrate that mixing models with convex weights correspond to random convex bodies formed by a Poisson process in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a fixed unit ball as the generating body, where the probability measure governing the weights is dual to the measure determining the distribution of the generating body. This connection enables us to characterize convex bodies that can be formed by such a process, which in turn leads to the distinction between integrally closed and non-integrally closed convex bodies. Furthermore, we explore the application of this framework to the study of random mixture models, focusing on the geometric interpretation of the measure governing the weights, as well as the use of closure properties to impose constraints on these measures, thereby extending the scope of models that can be analyzed. The development of new algorithms based on the closure of visibility of a body from a point is also presented. The relationship between mixing models and stochastic convex geometry offers a potential answer to the question of whether certain measures, such as Dirichlet measures, are the unique measures governing weights in mixture models, where the number of components is known. The research is further illustrated with numerical examples of drawdown mixture density estimation and the algorithm for visibility closure. We investigated the electronic and magnetic structure of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO$_{2}$ using periodic density functional theory. As the concentration varies from point defects to layered distributions, we examined different configurations of C and N in the TiO$_{2}$ crystal lattice. Our study analyzed doped TiO$_{2}$ in both its intrinsic and photoexcited state, as well as the effect of different surface orientations. Our results show that substitutional silicon-like behavior is unique to nitrogen defects when embedded deep within the TiO$_{2}$ lattice, where a single electron resides in an isolated orbital and the electron closely resembles a 2p hole. Furthermore, we found that nitrogen defects possess inherent magnetic properties and exhibit both spin and orbital magnetic behavior, primarily influenced by localized electron interactions and the lack of symmetry due to the crystal lattice. Conversely, surface-embedded nitrogen defects display both N 2p and Ti 3d bonding and tend to lose their magnetic properties when saturated with oxygen. Our research indicates that both carbon and nitrogen defects have unique electronic and magnetic characteristics that can be controlled through concentration and surface orientation, potentially allowing for the creation of novel magnetic structures and enabling the modulation of their electronic properties through chemical means. This could lead to applications in photodynamics, catalysis, and memory storage. Finally, we propose that this study's results may be extended to other p-element doped TiO$_{2}$ materials, potentially uncovering a wide range of functional properties across this class of materials.

This study examines texture-fueled friction in liquids through a combined approach of experimental observation and mathematical analysis. Specifically, we observed the flow of liquid foams on surfaces with regularly spaced spines of different angles and widths. As a result, we were able to determine the change in texture-induced friction resulting from changing spine orientations and lengths. Our research reveals that surface-induced friction undergoes a significant increase when the size of the spines roughly matches the size of the air bubbles. Furthermore, we found that surface-induced friction can be highly variable, depending on the texture of the surface, when partially broken surfaces are used. Our findings are relevant to various issues involving the flow of liquids, including surface-induced friction in the human body, flows across rough surfaces in the environment, and the flow of liquids with embedded objects. Our research also highlights potential uses of textures that slow down the flow of liquids, such as antifouling surfaces or certain medications. Our study used a simplified model of surfaces and extracted key information from these models that is necessary for understanding and predicting texture-fueled friction in liquids. Our data and mathematical analysis provide valuable information for predicting and understanding texture-fueled friction in liquids, which can be applied to various technological and medical applications. Our research has demonstrated that air-bubble liquids, such as foams, offer a unique way to examine texture-fueled friction in liquids. Our study also introduced a new parameter called the "aspect ratio of spines" that provides a better explanation of texture-fueled friction in liquids. Our research on the flow of air-bubble liquids has shown that the flow of these liquids can be slowed down to a stop, which is an unprecedented finding. Our data on the flow of air-bubble liquids also demonstrated that the process can be reversed, allowing the flow of these liquids to resume. Our research has further discovered that surface-induced friction in air-bubble liquids is influenced by the presence of solid objects and has uncovered a previously unknown phenomenon called "texture-induced stagnation." Our study has also examined the flow of liquids with embedded objects and has discovered that the process of flow and stagnation can be repeated repeatedly. The steady-state behavior of a fluid interface moving under influence of a constant pressure difference in a Hele-Shaw cell, especially when it includes a corner formed by two parallel sides, has been well studied and can be described by a variety of methods. However, studies on a Hele-Shaw cell with a 90-degree corner, rotated at a high speed, and featuring a fluid interface with complex shapes, have been limited. In this work, we investigate the stability of a finger shaped interface in such a cell, focusing on the effects of low rotation rates, cell aspect ratios, and finger shapes on the interface's behavior. We developed a model that describes this situation and through calculations, we explored various scenarios. Our findings show that in a rotated Hele-Shaw cell with a corner, the interface's shape can become non-smooth, but only when the cell's aspect ratio meets a certain criterion that depends on the rate of rotation. Additionally, we discovered that the interface's stability at low pressure differences or small radius curves can be unstable, but only results in the interface shifting towards a stable, smooth shape. Furthermore, we found that the interface's shape in a rotated Hele-Shaw cell with a corner is sensitive to the conditions of its surrounding environment. In the experimental section, we implemented a technique called thermocapillary fingging to disturb the interface and then allowed it to return to its original state; our results matched the predictions made from our model and the interface's shape changed slowly over time due to a subtle effect called surface tension gradient driven shifting. In a cell with a curved side, the interface broke up into branches, while in a cell with two straight sides and a small gap, the interface shifted towards a more stable shape but only at very low rates of rotation. In a cell with two straight sides and a large gap, the interface changed shape slowly due to the surface tension gradient. In the final experiment, we changed the cell's aspect ratio and observed the interface's behavior change accordingly. This work provides an in-depth analysis of a complex situation that has not been well studied before. In addition, we have made some subtle effects, that have been previously overlooked, visible and worthy of further investigation. This work has also implied some possible connections between some other complex and unrelated situations that have also been previously overlooked. This work has been conducted in a way that allows for easy replication and has provided some practical applications in designing certain industrial situations. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these consequences, we use effective field theories to describe these phenomena. Specifically, we examined the impact of J/ψ decay into invisible matter within the frameworks of effective field theories that incorporate light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. We analyzed two scenarios: one where the invisible component is comprised of two photons and one neutrino, and another where it consists of two photons and two neutrinos. We then compared these to the general case of invisible matter, assuming only that the consequence is modified by the angular distribution of the photon. We further explored these consequences within effective field theories of light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. In the case of light sterile neutrinos, we analyzed short-lived hadronic decays and both short-lived and long-lived leptonic decays. For sub-GeV dark matter, we examined short-lived hadronic and leptonic decays. We established lower bounds on the mass of new physics in effective field theories of light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter based on J/ψ decay into invisible matter. These limits vary by scenario: for hadronic decays they are 7.0 GeV for hadronic decays and 5.5 GeV for leptonic decays within light sterile neutrino effective field theories, while for sub-GeV dark matter they are 5.5 GeV for hadronic decays and 4.5 GeV for leptonic decays. We also noted that in effective field theories of light sterile neutrinos, the limit on hadronic decays is essentially the same as that for leptonic decays, and that in effective field theories of sub-GeV dark matter, the limit on hadronic decays is essentially the same as that for leptonic decays. We further found that in effective field theories of light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter, the limit on hadronic decays is higher than that for leptonic decays, and that in effective field theories of light sterile neutrinos, the limit on radiative decays is lower than that for hadronic decays, and that in effective field theories of sub-GeV dark matter, the limit on radiative decays is lower than that for hadronic decays. We also analyzed the consequences of J/ψ decay into invisible matter for the effective field theories of light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter

This research investigates the long-term behavior of a specific type of random walk model, denoted as (SDRW), characterized by a constant speed $c$ and a local time parameter $L_t$. We establish that the probability $P_r$ that the random walk $X_t$ exceeds a threshold $r$ eventually occurs globally, with this probability being directly proportional to the square root of the local time $L_t$ for the case where the speed $c$ is less than 1, and proportional to the square root of the difference $(1-c)^2L_t$ for the case where the speed $c$ is greater than 1. Furthermore, we derive specific probability bounds $P_r \geq \frac{1-c}{\sqrt{1-c^2}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1-c^2L_t}{r}}$ and $P_r \geq \frac{1-c}{\sqrt{1-c^2}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1-c^2L_t}{r}}$ for the two respective cases. These results extend and improve existing probability bounds found in literature, specifically for the simple random walk case where the speed $c$ is less than 1, and provide novel analysis for the corresponding biased random walk case. The research involves developing a new stochastic inequality based on a specific system of random walk and a related system of branching processes, as well as an auxiliary process known as the $2$-$M$-process. The results for the SDRW case were obtained using a combination of existing literature results, specifically the duality relationship established by the authors in their previous research, and a related persistence inequality also found in that previous research. The research can be extended to include related results for a random walk model with periodic speed, as well as bi-dimensional random walks, along specific directions. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively evaluating nucleus segmentation solutions is challenging due to the lack of precise golden standards from pathologists. Generally, pathologists agree on the overall diagnosis but may have differing opinions on details such as cell classification, especially in cases like lung cancer, where the distinction between different cell types is critical. As a result, evaluating nucleus segmentation solutions is often difficult, as there is no universal golden standard to compare against. In response to these challenges, a new two-stage network called W-Net has been developed to enhance nucleus segmentation by combining low-resolution, mask-label propagation, and deep learning techniques. According to our research, W-Net delivers superior nucleus segmentation results, as demonstrated in our experiments using data sets like CTC and LUNA. Nonetheless, what is more significant about this network is its ability to classify cells and determine their location within images, without any need for further segmentation. Moreover, W-Net facilitates evaluation solutions like nucleus annotation, image reconstruction, and cell classification, without any need for additional information other than trained models. Consequently, this new network has far-reaching applications beyond simply identifying cells, including tasks like image reconstruction, cell classification, and more, all without the requirement for additional supervision. In addition to its technical merits, our findings also provide valuable insights for evaluating nucleus segmentation solutions, as well as cancer cell classification, in areas like lung cancer. We have made W-Net's source code available to the public, in the hope that it will serve as a foundation for further innovation and improvement. Moreover, we have detailed the evaluation protocol and data sets used in our research, in order to facilitate replication and comparison by our peers. Deep Neural Network techniques, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained remarkable precision in tackling complex graph-level classifications and predictions. However, the underlying mathematical principles of these networks, particularly the connection to the theory of Probing and the generation of spectral convolution, are not well understood by the community. In order to address this knowledge gap, we offer a non-technical introduction to the fundamentals of GCNNs, explaining how the networks work through a simple and intuitive method called'matched filtering'. This approach, rooted in linear signal processing, provides a clear mathematical representation of the networks' operations, revealing their direct relationship to the Fourier transform and the application of the Probing theory. By transforming the GCNNs in this form, we are able to derive important properties of the networks, offering insights that can be used to improve their performance. Finally, we demonstrate how this approach can be used to modify the GCNNs, leading to a significant improvement in accuracy in various classification tasks. The simple and intuitive framework of matched filtering provides a accessible foundation for understanding the principles of GCNNs, accessible to researchers with a background in signal processing rather than deep learning. The approach presented here is applicable to both shallow and deep GCNNs, offering a general framework that can be tailored to specific tasks and networks. The code for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/abolfazlR/Matched-Filtering-GCNN. The advice and guidance offered in this paper are applicable to a wide range of networks, including GCNN, GCNN+, Graph Attention Network, and Graph Attention Network+, as well as other networks that can be treated as GCNN. To address this limitation, we introduce the virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) method, an advanced technique that enhances the signal reception and accurately estimates the lateral shift with increased precision. The findings suggest that the VSSA method delivers a 14% improvement in score ratings compared to the SA technique, and also supports the efficient use of hardware in ultrasound systems. The proposed VSSA method can be used for the safe clinical application of elastography in areas like cancer treatment monitoring. The method has a relatively simple hardware requirement and can be implemented on existing ultrasound systems with minor software modifications. Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. In the context of data analysis, a variation of the $k$-centers problem is often utilized to create a simplified representation of complex data sets. This problem involves identifying the minimum number of points (clusters), within a specified distance threshold, that are necessary to represent the original data. The problem has been extensively studied for static data sets, however, this paper focuses on the dynamic variation of the problem where the data set and distance threshold may change over time. We have achieved notable improvements in creating algorithms for solving the dynamic $k$-centers problem in high-dimensional spaces. Specifically, we have developed innovative techniques to solve the problem for data sets in high-dimensional spaces and to update the solution for data sets that change over time in high-dimensional spaces. These techniques are not only efficient but also minimize the increase in the required number of points to represent the data set after each update. We believe our approaches to be among the best possible strategies for solving the dynamic $k$-centers problem in high-dimensional spaces. In the specific case of Euclidean distances, we have a parameter-free algorithm that runs in a time of $O(1)$ per update and requires the addition of a constant number of points to the solution for each dimensionary change in the data set or distance threshold. In the general case of arbitrary distances, we have an algorithm that runs in a time of $O(\sqrt{k \log k})$ per update and requires the addition of a factor of $\max\{k,\log k\}$ to the solution for each change in the data set or distance threshold. We have also investigated static versions of the problem in the context of distributed systems and have obtained results that are applicable to these scenarios. The approach we have taken to the problem, we believe, is characterized by innovative techniques that are likely to be beneficial for solving other challenging problems in the field of computational geometry. The paper is concluded with an examination of these innovative techniques in the context of static and dynamic problems in the context of distributed systems and with the presentation of an open problem that we have termed as the $\gamma$-factor problem. The approach we have taken to solving this problem is also presented in the paper. The results we have obtained for the Euclidean distances are presented in the paper as the solution to the problem that was previously posted on the online platform arXiv. We then develop a decision-based approach using recursive formulations to address the hierarchical problem, and establish the connection between this approach and a hierarchical representation via the Nash equilibrium. Additionally, we establish the relationship between state categories (e.g. evader-winnable or defender-winnable) and the value functions associated with each state. Moreover, we provide a numerical solution to hierarchical models and demonstrate the efficacy of our method through simulated evader-defender problems. As an extension, we apply the hierarchical framework to a representation of the Stochastic Ski Resort domain, a complex domain characterized by multiple evaders, spatially-dependent action outcomes, and tree-like terrain, and show that this approach yields comparable performance to a simpler version of the domain. Compared to traditional methods, EVBA demonstrates significant gains in computational efficiency, achieving a 90% average reduction in calculation time while maintaining accurate results for various observables in both the high and low momentum limits. Nonetheless, some technical challenges remain in implementing EVBA for certain observables in the low-momentum limit, particularly with the increasing number of calculations required for smaller scattering angles in muon colliders. To overcome these difficulties, we propose alternative, more efficient methods of calculating EVBA in these scenarios. Moreover, our findings indicate that EVBA can be effectively employed for evaluating scattering amplitudes on existing supercomputing infrastructure, with further optimization potential to expand its applicability to an even broader range of computations. The Efficient Vector Boson Approximation can be employed in various contexts, including as a tool for studying strong interaction effects and as a fast generator for future experiments, and we anticipate its value increasing further as more powerful computing resources become available in the future. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to catastrophic forgetting of initial tasks as new ones are
introduced. To overcome this, we show that isolating sub-networks of the dynamics model significantly increases the effectiveness of multi-task reinforcement learning, allowing for a rich exchange of knowledge between tasks without forgetting. We validate our findings with multiple experiments, demonstrating the superiority of isolated networks in both simple and challenging multi-task scenarios. Our approach also scales to large datasets, as evident from our analysis. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for future research in multi-task reinforcement learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/PranavTyagi/MultiTaskDynamics.

We introduce a novel model where four mobile agents, inspired by Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser, navigate through the plane to gather at a specifically designated meeting point. Each agent's path is defined by a differential equation based on the directions they take, with the goal of achieving a particular angle between their trajectories. We investigate several key aspects of this system in the context of the plane, including its structure, the set of possible states it can occupy, and the gathering scenario with four agents. Our analysis reveals that the system's state space consists of two distinct components: a planar disk and a semi-torus. In the case of the plane and the semi-torus, we determine the conditions under which the system can gather seamlessly. However, on the annulus, we find that the system's behavior is more complex and depends on the specific parameters, while on the circle, the system cannot gather for most of the time. Our study also discusses the relationship between the system's state and the angles formed by the agents' paths, as well as the impact of adding a boundary to the system. Furthermore, we provide numerical examples to demonstrate the effects of different parameters on the system's performance. Lastly, we offer an interpretation of this model as a metaphor for the interconnection of different mathematical formalisms. The underlying system can be extended to mimic the behavior of mobile robots in the presence of obstacles, as well as in the presence of errors or delays. The model has significant implications for the theory of partial differential equations, specifically in the context of the Birkhoff normal form, and may find applications in the study of nonlinear Schrödinger equations, as well as in the analysis of the complexity of finite state automata. The associated source code is available at https://github.com/mbartuccelli/GTRC. The corresponding numerical toolbox can be used to solve a broad range of PDEs, including those associated with the circular Foucault theorem, the Geyer-Rossler metric, and the Navier-Stokes equations, among others. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on capturing the posterior distribution of all possible images. We propose a new algorithm that generates a parameter space where the conditional GAN can produce high-quality samples that follow the desired posterior distribution. The proposed method produces a compact representation of the posterior distribution by incorporating a sparse regularization technique, resulting in a set of representative samples that capture the posterior's key characteristics, such as data statistics, structural elements and color information. We validate our method against competing approaches and demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to low-dose MRI reconstruction and image deblurring techniques. The proposed algorithm outperformed existing methods in terms of quantitative assessment and produced visually plausible results in both cases. This research paper examines a specific type of surface, called an invariant surface, within a broad class of dynamical systems, specifically those governed by fractional-order differential equations. Invariant surfaces have a special property where their composition with the dynamical system results in the same dynamics as the original system. However, our key finding proves that there are dynamical systems, specifically those of fractional order, for which no invariant surfaces exist. This breakthrough achieves two significant goals: it confirms a long-standing conjecture regarding planar dynamical systems, while also extending that consensus to a more intricate system comprised of multiple dimensions. Furthermore, our research reveals that the absence of invariant surfaces in a given system is always indicative of its stability properties. In the case of planar systems, this translates to the system's stability being classified as asymptotic rather than exponential. For more complex systems of a higher dimensional nature, we uncover a more intricate relationship between the system's stability and the specific fractional dimensions in which it operates. Specifically, we find that these systems exhibit exponential stability when operating within a fractional dimension of order one, whereas they demonstrate asymptotic stability when operating within a fractional dimension of order two. Lastly, we also uncover a more general criterion for system stability that can be applied to any fractional dimension. Our key findings are then validated through numerical analysis of various fractional systems. Our research contributes a novel approach to detecting stability in dynamical systems, specifically those of a fractional nature, by utilizing numerical tools to visualize the nonexistence of invariant surfaces and thereby inferring the system's stability properties. We also explore and report on some notable examples of fractional systems, including those with constant time delays, periodic systems, and chaotic systems, among others. Our work further discovers a related concept called an invariant curve in these systems and sheds light on the key that leads to its nonexistence. Our approach to detecting stability in dynamical systems, specifically those of a fractional nature, can be found in the form of an executable code available online. Our research paper is organized as follows: the mathematical background and definition of invariant surfaces are presented in Chapter 2, while Chapter 3 delves into the nonexistence of invariant surfaces and its implications for dynamical systems. Chapter 4 discusses the relationship between the system's stability and the nonexistence of invariant surfaces, with specific examples and case studies detailed in Chapter 5. Our work is then summarized in Chapter 6. The appendix at the end of the paper includes some important mathematical proofs. Our research paper is targeted towards a broad audience of mathematicians and scientists

The pulsar B1133+16, located at a sky position of 11.82 ddeg, exhibits significant variability in its pulse shape, likely caused by interactions with the interstellar medium. Pulsar scintillation observations at 1.4 GHz over a 20-year period for this pulsar reveal significant changes in pulse shape, wide-bandhood, and total flux. Pulsar scintillation indices show a yearly change and are similar to those found for the pulsars B1933+16 and B2117+41, indicating a similar level of scintillation effect. Analyzing pulse shape variations, we find that the average shape changes significantly over 20 years, with changes observable in up to 50% of pulses. In addition, we find distinct, persistent variations in pulse shape in the frequency domain, likely caused by material patches in the line of sight. Estimated dimensions of these patches range from 0.0003 to 0.003 parsecs in length. Combining data from different years, we find that the pulse shape variations depend on the sky position, with changes more pronounced at lower ecliptic latitudes. This could be explained by variations in the density of the interstellar plasma within the Galactic plane. On the other hand, the relationship between the size of the pulse shape variations and the distance the pulsar travels in its orbit is consistent with the model that attributes these variations to the Earth's motion. Therefore, we interpret this as a global effect caused by the distribution of the free electron density within the line of sight to the pulsar, influenced by the Earth's motion and the density of the Galactic plane. This leads to a better understanding of the structure and dynamics of the interstellar medium within the solar neighborhood. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through an innovative pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural network. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation by utilizing a deeply cascaded autoregressive architecture, yet its limited pitch control results from converted learned features instead of direct pitch influence. To overcome this constraint, we introduce a pitch-dependent expanded convolutional network where each stage consists of multiple convolutional layers with different filter banks, whose inputs are combined using vector-based attention. The proposed model excels at generating speech with varied pitch patterns and periodic signals like piano sounds, demonstrating the versatility of QPNet in multiple domains. The bicategorical invariants theory has its foundations rooted in the theory of subfields within the extension fields, as identified by Galois group actions on fields. Extending these concepts to the realm of shadows, we define the shadows of a field with respect to a Galois extension, and demonstrate how they are inherently associated with the Picard-Vessier system of the extension. Furthermore, we establish that shadows are conservative in nature, implying that they behave conservatively under the restriction of subfields. Utilizing shadows, we establish a direct connection between the Picard-Vessier system of a global function field and the Galois group of a specific extension field. Moreover, we show that in the global function field setting, the shadows can be viewed as an advancement of the bicategorical invariants theory, building upon the existing framework of Picard-Vessier systems. Additionally, we provide a precise characterization of the shadows associated with the Abelian extensions of a global function field. In a separate context, we show that the shadows can be applied to the bi categorie invariants theory of the finite fields, thereby extending the bicategorical invariants theory to the realm of finite fields. Lastly, we discuss the fundamental relationship between the shadows and the Picard-Vessier systems, thereby paving the way for potential future work involving the bi categorie invariants theory of the local function fields. In a broader sense, this research can be seen as an expansion of the bicategorical invariants theory, with its underlying principles rooted in the theory of subfields within the extension fields, as analyzed by Galois group actions on fields. Our primary goal in this research is to demonstrate the challenging nature of a visual noise localization task, which can be achieved either automatically by training a single model to distinguish between different types of noises or manually by compiling a collection of noise images from various sources. We've assembled a dedicated dataset called VNL, comprising 50,000 training images and 10,000 testing images, which represents a significant step towards addressing this challenging task. Our findings, which outperform existing benchmarks, are evidenced by a model we've developed which achieves an 82% accuracy rate in identifying noise types and a 73% rate of correctly determining the orientation of noise patterns. Moreover, our model demonstrates applicability in noise reduction and image forensics applications, offering competitive results when compared to customized models and industry-standard approaches. The comprehensive evaluation includes detailed subgroup analyses, validation of our results through multiple experiments, and a novel approach to evaluate noise localization automatically. The code and model for this project are available at https://github.com/ghrua/VNL. The VNL dataset is available for download at https://ghrua.github.io/VNL.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been driven by their application in representing complex and non-euclidean data, and there's a growing interest in developing GNNs that can operate on graphs with a positive definite manifold. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for defining GNNs on positive definite manifolds, and demonstrate the versatility of this framework by incorporating multiple positive definite manifolds within a single graph. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on datasets that incorporate linear subspaces, non-linear subspaces, and circular manifolds, and our method is found to surpass existing techniques. We also explore the properties of our model and discover that it is influenced by a variety of factors, including the network's depth, width, and initialization, as well as the hyperparameters of the optimizer. Our research also enables us to successfully train a GNN on a complex dataset with a multi-linear manifold. We hope that this work will serve as a foundation for future research on GNNs, especially those dealing with heterogeneous data and multi-manifold graphs. Our code is available at https://github.com/LC-1024/LGNNSimple.

This research focuses on a mathematical problem associated with a structural acoustic interaction, where we aim to determine the properties of a solid object based on sound wave data in the surrounding environment. A key obstacle in this endeavor is the complex nature of the data, which results from the object and its surrounding environment interacting with each other. To overcome this challenge, we first establish a theoretical foundation for a specific way of interacting objects and sound waves, based on a particular approach that involves a series of increasingly complex constructions. Ultimately, this framework enables us to develop a practical method for estimating the object's properties, which we demonstrate works effectively in a real-world scenario. The methodology we've developed and the associated mathematical proofs both rely heavily on the use of a specialized operator called a singular trace, which is a crucial component in defining the object's properties and determining the error associated with their estimation. The development of our inverse problem solution also involves developing a new type of regularization technique called the singular trace method, which provides a more precise and comprehensive framework for solving similar inverse problems that involve the interaction of sound waves and solid objects. The research mentioned above was originally published in the journal Inverse Problems, volume 37, issue 1, 2021, article id 015012, and in the journal Mathematics of Computation, volume 90, issue 329, pages 155-185, 2021. The associated algorithms have been successfully implemented and are available for public use. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, we establish that our model's impulse control
equation aligns with the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting model, offering a more
advanced analysis of impulsivity that extends beyond its standard definition. 
This model's capacity to account for deviations from impulsivity is demonstrated
through additional empirical support, and it also enables a deeper understanding
of how and why individuals make choices based on hyperbolic delay discounting. 
This model has numerous potential applications in various fields including
psychology, economics, and sociology. Finally, we outline future research
directions for further validating the model and exploring its implications. This
includes analyzing its connection to the Tsallis entropy, investigating how it
relates to other discounting models, and determining the factors that influence
impulsivity.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By combining spin-orbit coupling and strong interaction, we find that the $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ mixals form a single band with an unusual distortion, comparable to experiments and calculations for 4d and 5d materials, including RuO2, MoO3, ReO3, and TaO3, CaTaO3, and SrTaO3. This approach also allows us to classify the materials as either high- or low-energy distortion types, demonstrating how spin-orbit coupling can shift the energy distortions from 4d to 5d materials. Additionally, we study the phase diagram of a single-band model formed by $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ mixals, revealing an insulating phase gap in the intermediate interaction strength regime along with phase transitions to either a Mott insulating or a metallic phase. This pattern is unaffected by spin-orbit coupling or whether it's a 4d or 5d material. Furthermore, we find that the mixals can form a 2D Fermi surface in a TaO3-type material with small on-site interaction, contrasting with the experimentally observed insulating behavior of this material, suggesting that the on-site interaction might be larger than previously thought, or that the band is affected by other factors such as structural distortions. This could also explain the disconnection between the small spin-orbit coupling and the presence of magnetic order in this and other materials. This research predicts a class of materials with unusual $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing distortion patterns, and suggests possible experimental studies of TaO3, focusing on the mixals of a particular 5d transition metal oxide. A more general theory of the phase diagram could potentially be applicable to other materials, based solely on the single-band $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixals formed through strong interaction and spin-orbit coupling, without reference to specific materials. This general phase diagram shows distinct transition points at both weak and strong interaction limits, which could be tested or validated by future experiments or calculations. Using advanced neural styling tools for photo editing, we investigate the potential risks they pose to medical diagnosis based on X-ray images. To explore this concern, we developed a system that systematically alters chest X-rays to simulate the effects of common respiratory illnesses. Our approach combines a neural styling tool with a quality assurance process to produce precise and realistic edits. We evaluated this system by examining the ability of machine learning models to accurately diagnose five different respiratory conditions from edited X-rays. The results show that, despite producing more uncertain diagnoses, the machine learning models can still effectively identify these conditions with a high degree of accuracy from edited images. We believe this finding has important implications for using neural styling tools in medical settings and provides a foundation for future research into illness simulation and manipulation of medical images. We are sharing our code and editing tool with the community to facilitate further innovation in this area. We recently expanded the tool to edit lung biopsy images in addition to X-rays. The potential applications of this tool extend beyond diagnosis and could be useful for simulating the effects of different treatments or the progression of diseases. The code for the tool is available at https://github.com/ghristy/respix. The edited images presented in this paper are fictional and not actual patient data.
